chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — London. A street
paragraphs: Enter Richard, Duke of Gloucester, alone.

RICHARD. Now the winter of our discontent has turned to glorious summer, thanks to this son of York, King Edward. All the clouds that hung over our house are buried deep in the ocean. Our brows are now wreathed with victory. Our battered weapons hang up as memorials. Our harsh war-alarms have become merry gatherings, and our dreadful marches have become pleasant dances. War, with his grim face, has smoothed out his wrinkles. Instead of riding armored warhorses to terrify his enemies, he now capers nimbly in a lady's bedroom to the lustful pleasure of a lute. But I was not shaped for games like these. I was not made to flirt with a mirror. I am roughly stamped, and I lack the majesty of love to strut in front of a wanton, swaying girl. I am cheated of my fair proportions, robbed of good looks by cheating nature. I am deformed and unfinished, sent into this breathing world before my time, barely half made, and so lame and ill-fashioned that dogs bark at me as I limp past them. Why, in this weak, piping time of peace, I have no pleasure to pass the time, unless it is to spy my shadow in the sun and talk at length about my own deformity. And so, since I cannot be a lover to enjoy these fine, smooth-talking days, I am determined to be a villain and hate the idle pleasures of these days. I have laid plots, dangerous openings to my scheme, using drunken prophecies, slanders and dreams, to set my brother Clarence and the King in deadly hatred of each other. And if King Edward is as honest and just as I am sly, false and treacherous, then Clarence will be shut up tight this very day because of a prophecy that says a "G" will murder Edward's heirs. Dive down, my thoughts, into my soul. Here comes Clarence.
Enter Clarence, guarded and Brakenbury.
Brother, good day. What does this armed guard mean, waiting on your Grace?
CLARENCE. His Majesty, out of concern for my safety, has appointed this escort to take me to the Tower.
RICHARD. For what reason?
CLARENCE. Because my name is George.

RICHARD. Alas, my lord, that is no fault of yours. For that, he should lock up your godfathers. Oh, perhaps his Majesty means for you to be christened again in the Tower. But what is going on, Clarence? May I know?

CLARENCE. Yes, Richard, when I know myself, for I swear I don't yet. But as far as I can learn, he listens to prophecies and dreams. He picks the letter G out of the alphabet and says a wizard told him that his heirs would be disinherited by someone with a "G." Since my name George begins with a G, he concludes in his mind that I am the one. These, as I hear, and trifles like them, have moved his Highness to lock me up now.

RICHARD. Why, this is what happens when men are ruled by women. It is not the King who sends you to the Tower. It is his wife, Lady Grey, Clarence, who pushes him to this extreme. Was it not she, and that worshipful gentleman Antony Woodville, her brother there, who made him send Lord Hastings to the Tower, from which he was released this very day? We are not safe, Clarence. We are not safe.

CLARENCE. By heaven, I think no man is secure except the Queen's relatives, and the night-walking messengers who trudge between the King and Mistress Shore. Didn't you hear what a humble beggar Lord Hastings was to her for his release?

RICHARD. By humbly pleading to her divinity, my Lord Chamberlain won his freedom. I'll tell you what: I think our way, if we want to stay in the King's favor, is to be her men and wear her uniform. She and that jealous, worn-out widow, the Queen, ever since our brother made them gentlewomen, are mighty gossips in our kingdom.
BRAKENBURY. I beg both your Graces to pardon me. His Majesty has strictly ordered that no man, whatever his rank, may speak privately with your brother.

RICHARD. Very well. If it pleases you, Brakenbury, you may share in anything we say. We speak no treason, man. We say the King is wise and virtuous, and his noble Queen is well along in years, fair, and not jealous. We say that Shore's wife has a pretty foot, a cherry lip, a bonny eye and an exceedingly pleasing tongue. And we say that the Queen's relatives have been made gentlefolk. What do you say, sir? Can you deny any of this?
BRAKENBURY. I have nothing to do with this, my lord.
RICHARD. Nothing to do with Mistress Shore? I tell you, fellow, the man who does nothing with her, except one, had better do it in secret and alone.
BRAKENBURY. What one, my lord?
RICHARD. Her husband, you rascal! Would you betray me?
BRAKENBURY. I beg your Grace to pardon me, and besides, please end your conversation with the noble Duke.
CLARENCE. We know your orders, Brakenbury, and will obey.

RICHARD. We are the Queen's outcasts and must obey. Brother, farewell. I will go to the King. Whatever you want me to do, even if it means calling King Edward's widow "sister," I will do it to set you free. Meanwhile, this deep disgrace between brothers touches me deeper than you can imagine.
CLARENCE. I know it pleases neither of us.
RICHARD. Well, your imprisonment will not be long. I will free you, or else take your place in prison. Meanwhile, be patient.
CLARENCE. I have no choice. Farewell.
[_Exeunt Clarence, Brakenbury and guard._]

RICHARD. Go, tread the path you will never walk back. Simple, plain Clarence, I love you so much that I will soon send your soul to heaven, if heaven will accept the gift from our hands. But who comes here? The newly freed Hastings?
Enter Lord Hastings.
HASTINGS. A good day to my gracious lord.
RICHARD. The same to my good Lord Chamberlain. You are well welcome to the open air. How did your lordship put up with prison?
HASTINGS. With patience, noble lord, as prisoners must. But I will live, my lord, to thank the men who caused my imprisonment.
RICHARD. No doubt, no doubt, and so will Clarence too. For those who were your enemies are his, and they have had as much influence over the King against him as against you.
HASTINGS. It is more pity that eagles should be caged while kites and buzzards hunt freely.
RICHARD. What news from outside?
HASTINGS. No news abroad is as bad as what we have at home. The King is sickly, weak and gloomy, and his physicians fear greatly for him.
RICHARD. Now, by Saint John, that news is bad indeed. Oh, he has kept a bad diet for a long time and overindulged his royal body. It is very grievous to think about. Where is he? In his bed?
HASTINGS. He is.
RICHARD. Go ahead of me, and I will follow you.
[_Exit Hastings._]

He cannot live, I hope, and must not die until George is packed off to heaven by post-horse. I'll go in and stir up the King's hatred of Clarence with lies backed by weighty arguments. And if my deep plan does not fail, Clarence will not have another day to live. Once that is done, God can take King Edward to his mercy and leave the world for me to bustle in. For then I'll marry Warwick's youngest daughter. What does it matter that I killed her husband and her father? The quickest way to make it up to the girl is to become her husband and her father. And I will, not so much for love as for another secret, private purpose, which I can reach only by marrying her. But I am running ahead of my horse to market. Clarence still breathes. Edward still lives and reigns. When they are gone, then I must count my gains.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — London. Another street
paragraphs: Enter the corse of King Henry the Sixth, with Halberds to guard it, Lady Anne, being the mourner, Tressel and Berkeley and other Gentlemen.

ANNE. Set down, set down your honorable load, if honor can be wrapped in a coffin, while I mourn for a while, as is my duty, the untimely fall of virtuous Lancaster. Poor, key-cold body of a holy king. Pale ashes of the house of Lancaster. You bloodless remnant of that royal blood. Let me call on your ghost to hear the laments of poor Anne, wife to your Edward, your slaughtered son. He was stabbed by the same hand that made these wounds. Look, into these windows that let out your life I pour the helpless balm of my poor eyes. Oh, cursed be the hand that made these holes. Cursed be the heart that had the heart to do it. Cursed be the blood that let this blood out. May worse misfortune fall on that hated wretch who makes us wretched by your death than I can wish on adders, spiders, toads or any creeping, venomous thing alive. If he ever has a child, may it be born dead, monstrous and before its time, with an ugly, unnatural look that may frighten its hopeful mother at the sight, and may that child inherit his unhappiness. If he ever has a wife, may she be made more miserable by his death than I am by the death of my young lord and you. Now go on toward Chertsey with your holy load, taken from Saint Paul's to be buried there. And whenever you are tired of the weight, rest, while I mourn King Henry's body.
[_They take up the bier._]
Enter Richard, Duke of Gloucester.
RICHARD. Stop, you who carry the corpse, and set it down.
ANNE. What black magician conjures up this fiend to stop devoted, charitable deeds?
RICHARD. Villains, set down the corpse, or, by Saint Paul, I'll make a corpse of whoever disobeys!
GENTLEMAN. My lord, stand back and let the coffin pass.
RICHARD. Ill-mannered dog! Stand still when I command you! Lift your halberd away from my chest, or by Saint Paul I'll strike you down at my feet and kick you, beggar, for your boldness.
[_They set down the bier._]

ANNE. What, do you tremble? Are you all afraid? Alas, I don't blame you, for you are mortal, and mortal eyes cannot endure the devil. Begone, you dreadful servant of hell! You had power only over his mortal body. You cannot have his soul, so go away.
RICHARD. Sweet saint, for charity's sake, don't be so bad-tempered.

ANNE. Foul devil, for God's sake, go away and do not trouble us. You have turned the happy earth into your hell and filled it with cursing cries and deep outcries. If you enjoy looking at your wicked deeds, look at this sample of your butchery. Oh, gentlemen, see, see how dead Henry's wounds open their clotted mouths and bleed afresh! Blush, blush, you lump of foul deformity, for it is your presence that draws this blood out of cold, empty veins where no blood lives. Your inhuman, unnatural deeds provoke this most unnatural flood. O God, who made this blood, avenge his death! O earth, who drinks this blood, avenge his death! Either let heaven strike the murderer dead with lightning, or let the earth gape open wide and swallow him alive, as you swallow the blood of this good King, which his hell-ruled arm has butchered.
RICHARD. Lady, you know none of the rules of charity, which pays back good for bad and blessings for curses.
ANNE. Villain, you know neither the law of God nor of man. No beast is so fierce that it does not know some touch of pity.
RICHARD. But I know none, and therefore I am no beast.
ANNE. Oh, how wonderful, when devils tell the truth!
RICHARD. More wonderful when angels are so angry. Divine perfection of a woman, be so kind as to let me clear myself of these supposed crimes by explaining the circumstances.
ANNE. Spreading infection of a man, be so kind as to let me accuse your cursed self of these known evils by explaining the circumstances.
RICHARD. You are fairer than any tongue can say. Let me have some patient time to excuse myself.
ANNE. You are fouler than any heart can imagine. The only excuse you can make that will pass is to hang yourself.
RICHARD. By such despair I would be accusing myself.
ANNE. And by despairing you will be excused, for taking just vengeance on yourself, who did unjust slaughter on others.
RICHARD. Suppose I did not kill them?
ANNE. Then suppose they were not killed. But they are dead, and by you, devilish slave.
RICHARD. I did not kill your husband.
ANNE. Why then, he is alive.
RICHARD. No, he is dead, and killed by Edward's hand.
ANNE. You lie in your foul throat. Queen Margaret saw your murderous sword smoking with his blood, the same sword you once aimed at her breast, until your brothers knocked the point aside.
RICHARD. I was provoked by her slanderous tongue, which laid their guilt on my guiltless shoulders.
ANNE. You were provoked by your bloody mind, which never dreams of anything but butchery. Did you not kill this King?
RICHARD. I grant it.
ANNE. You grant it, you hedgehog? Then may God grant me also that you are damned for that wicked deed. Oh, he was gentle, mild and virtuous.
RICHARD. All the better for the King of Heaven, who has him.
ANNE. He is in heaven, where you will never come.
RICHARD. Let him thank me, who helped to send him there, for he was fitter for that place than for earth.
ANNE. And you are fit for no place but hell.
RICHARD. Yes, one other place, if you will let me name it.
ANNE. Some dungeon.
RICHARD. Your bedroom.
ANNE. May the room where you lie have bad rest!
RICHARD. So it will, madam, until I lie with you.
ANNE. I hope so.

RICHARD. I know so. But, gentle Lady Anne, let us leave this sharp exchange of wits and move to a slower manner. Isn't the one who caused the untimely deaths of these Plantagenets, Henry and Edward, as much to blame as the executioner?
ANNE. You were the cause, and the most accursed result.
RICHARD. Your beauty was the cause of that result. Your beauty haunted me in my sleep, driving me to undertake the death of all the world, so long as I might live one hour in your sweet bosom.
ANNE. If I thought that, I tell you, murderer, these nails would tear that beauty from my cheeks.
RICHARD. These eyes could not bear to see that beauty ruined. You would not mar it while I stood by. As all the world is cheered by the sun, so I am by that beauty. It is my day, my life.
ANNE. May black night cover your day, and death your life.
RICHARD. Do not curse yourself, fair creature. You are both.
ANNE. I wish I were, so I could be revenged on you.
RICHARD. It is an unnatural quarrel, to take revenge on the man who loves you.
ANNE. It is a just and reasonable quarrel, to take revenge on the man who killed my husband.
RICHARD. The man who robbed you of your husband, lady, did it to help you to a better husband.
ANNE. A better one does not breathe on the earth.
RICHARD. He lives who loves you better than he could.
ANNE. Name him.
RICHARD. Plantagenet.
ANNE. Why, that was his name.
RICHARD. The very same name, but one of a better nature.
ANNE. Where is he?
RICHARD. Here.
[_She spits at him._]
Why do you spit at me?
ANNE. I wish it were deadly poison, for your sake.
RICHARD. Poison never came from so sweet a place.
ANNE. Poison never hung on a fouler toad. Out of my sight! You infect my eyes.
RICHARD. Your eyes, sweet lady, have infected mine.
ANNE. I wish they were basilisks, to strike you dead!

RICHARD. I wish they were, so that I might die at once. For now they kill me with a living death. Those eyes of yours have drawn salt tears from mine and shamed my eyes with a flood of childish drops. These eyes never shed a tear of pity, not when my father York and Edward wept to hear the piteous moan that Rutland made as black-faced Clifford shook his sword at him. Nor when your warlike father, like a child, told the sad story of my father's death, pausing twenty times to sob and weep, so that everyone standing by had cheeks as wet as trees drenched with rain. In that sad time my manly eyes scorned a humble tear. And what those sorrows could not draw out of them, your beauty has, and made them blind with weeping. I never begged from friend or enemy. My tongue never learned a sweet, smoothing word. But now your beauty is offered as my reward, my proud heart begs, and urges my tongue to speak.
[_She looks scornfully at him._]

Don't teach your lip such scorn. It was made for kissing, lady, not for such contempt. If your revengeful heart cannot forgive, look, here I lend you this sharp-pointed sword. If you will bury it in this faithful breast and let out the soul that adores you, I lay it bare to the deadly stroke, and humbly beg for death on my knee.
[_He kneels and lays his breast open; she offers at it with his sword._]
No, don't hesitate. I did kill King Henry, but it was your beauty that provoked me. Go on, finish it. It was I who stabbed young Edward, but it was your heavenly face that set me on.
[_She falls the sword._]
Pick up the sword again, or pick me up.
ANNE. Get up, you hypocrite. Though I wish you dead, I will not be your executioner.
RICHARD. Then tell me to kill myself, and I will do it.
ANNE. I have already.

RICHARD. That was in your rage. Say it again, and the moment you say it, this hand, which for love of you killed your love, will for love of you kill a far truer love. You will be an accomplice to both their deaths.
ANNE. I wish I knew your heart.
RICHARD. It is shown in my tongue.
ANNE. I fear both are false.
RICHARD. Then no man was ever true.
ANNE. Well, well, put away your sword.
RICHARD. Then say my peace is made with you.
ANNE. You will find that out later.
RICHARD. But may I live in hope?
ANNE. All men, I hope, live that way.
RICHARD. Be so kind as to wear this ring.
ANNE. To take is not to give.
[_He places the ring on her hand._]

RICHARD. Look how my ring circles your finger. In the same way your breast encloses my poor heart. Wear them both, for both are yours. And if your poor devoted servant may beg just one favor from your gracious hand, you will secure his happiness forever.
ANNE. What is it?

RICHARD. That you will be pleased to leave these sad tasks to the man who has the most reason to be the mourner, and go at once to Crosby Place. There, after I have solemnly buried this noble King at Chertsey monastery and wet his grave with my repentant tears, I will come to see you with all possible dutiful speed. For reasons I can't explain now, I beg you, grant me this favor.
ANNE. With all my heart, and it pleases me much to see that you have become so penitent. Tressel and Berkeley, come along with me.
RICHARD. Say farewell to me.
ANNE. That is more than you deserve. But since you teach me how to flatter you, imagine I have already said farewell.
[_Exeunt Lady Anne, Tressel and Berkeley._]
RICHARD. Sirs, take up the corpse.
GENTLEMAN. To Chertsey, noble lord?
RICHARD. No, to White Friars. Wait there for me.
[_Exeunt Halberds and Gentlemen with corse._]

Was ever woman wooed in such a mood? Was ever woman won in such a mood? I'll have her, but I won't keep her long. What! I, who killed her husband and his father, to win her in the very depth of her hatred, with curses in her mouth and tears in her eyes, with the bleeding proof of her hatred right beside us! I had God, her conscience and all these obstacles against me, and no friends to back my suit, only the plain devil and deceiving looks. And yet to win her, I'd bet the whole world against nothing! Ha! Has she already forgotten that brave prince Edward, her lord, whom I stabbed in my anger at Tewksbury about three months ago? A sweeter and lovelier gentleman, shaped in nature's generosity, young, brave, wise and no doubt truly royal, the wide world cannot offer again. And yet will she lower her eyes to me, who cut off the golden prime of this sweet prince and left her a widow in a sorrowful bed? To me, whose whole worth does not equal half of Edward's? To me, who limp and am misshapen like this? I'd bet my dukedom against a beggarly coin that I have been mistaken about my own appearance all this time! On my life, she finds, though I cannot, that I am a remarkably handsome man. I'll spend money on a looking-glass and hire a score or two of tailors to study fashions to dress my body. Since I have crept into my own good opinion, I will keep it up at some small cost. But first I'll send that fellow back into his grave, and then return, lamenting, to my love. Shine out, fair sun, until I have bought a glass, so that I can see my shadow as I pass.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — London. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: Enter Queen Elizabeth, the Marquess of Dorset, Lord Rivers and Lord Grey.
RIVERS. Have patience, madam. There is no doubt his Majesty will soon get back his usual health.
GREY. By taking it so badly, you make him worse. So for God's sake, take comfort and cheer his Grace with a bright, merry face.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. If he were dead, what would become of me?
GREY. No other harm than the loss of such a lord.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. The loss of such a lord includes every harm.
GREY. Heaven has blessed you with a fine son to comfort you when he is gone.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, he is young, and while he is a minor he is placed in the care of Richard Gloucester, a man who loves neither me nor any of you.
RIVERS. Is it settled that he will be Protector?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. It is decided, but not yet settled. But so it must be, if the King dies.
Enter Buckingham and Stanley, Earl of Derby.
GREY. Here come the Lords of Buckingham and Derby.
BUCKINGHAM. Good day to your royal Grace.
STANLEY. May God make your Majesty as joyful as you have been.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. The Countess of Richmond, my good Lord of Derby, will hardly say amen to your prayer. Yet, Derby, even though she is your wife and does not love me, be assured, good lord, that I do not hate you because of her proud arrogance.

STANLEY. I beg you, either do not believe the spiteful slanders of her false accusers, or, if she is accused by true report, put up with her weakness, which I think comes from a moody sickness and not from any deep-rooted malice.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Did you see the King today, my Lord of Derby?
STANLEY. The Duke of Buckingham and I have just now come from visiting his Majesty.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. How likely is it that he will get better, lords?
BUCKINGHAM. Madam, there is good hope. His Grace speaks cheerfully.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. God grant him health! Did you talk with him?
BUCKINGHAM. Yes, madam. He wants to make peace between the Duke of Gloucester and your brothers, and between them and my Lord Chamberlain. He has sent to summon them to his royal presence.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I wish all were well, but that will never be. I fear our happiness is at its height.
Enter Richard, Duke of Gloucester and Hastings.

RICHARD. They wrong me, and I will not stand for it! Who is it that complains to the King that I, if you please, am harsh and don't love them? By holy Paul, they love his Grace only lightly if they fill his ears with such quarrelsome rumors. Because I cannot flatter and look pleasant, smile in men's faces, smooth things over, deceive and cheat, bow with French nods and ape-like courtesy, I must be seen as a bitter enemy. Can't a plain man live and mean no harm, without his simple honesty being abused by silken, sly, insinuating knaves?
GREY. To whom in all this company does your Grace speak?

RICHARD. To you, who have neither honesty nor grace. When have I injured you? When did I wrong you? Or you? Or you? Or anyone in your faction? A plague on you all! His royal Grace, whom God preserve better than you would wish, can hardly be quiet for a breathing moment without you troubling him with your low complaints.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Brother of Gloucester, you misunderstand. The King, on his own royal initiative, and not provoked by any other petitioner, is aiming, perhaps, at the hatred you hold inside, which shows in your outward behavior toward my children, my brothers and me. That is why he sends for you, so that he may learn the ground of your ill will and thereby remove it.
RICHARD. I can't say. The world has grown so bad that wrens hunt where eagles dare not perch. Ever since every Jack became a gentleman, many a gentleman has been made a Jack.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Come, come, we know what you mean, brother Gloucester. You envy my rise, and my friends' rise. God grant we never need your help.

RICHARD. Meanwhile, God grants that we do need your help. Our brother is imprisoned by your doing, I am disgraced, and the nobility are held in contempt, while great promotions are handed out every day to ennoble people who were barely worth a single noble coin two days ago.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. By Him who raised me to this troubled height from the contented fortune I enjoyed, I never stirred up his Majesty against the Duke of Clarence. I have been an earnest advocate pleading for him. My lord, you do me shameful injury to drag me falsely into these vile suspicions.
RICHARD. You may deny that you were not the means of my Lord Hastings' recent imprisonment.
RIVERS. She may, my lord, for —

RICHARD. She may, Lord Rivers! Why, who doesn't know that? She may do more than deny it, sir. She may help you to many fine promotions, and then deny that she lent a hand, and credit those honors to your own great merit. What may she not do? She may, yes, indeed, she may —
RIVERS. What, indeed, may she?
RICHARD. What, indeed, may she? Marry a king, a bachelor, and a handsome youngster too. Truly, your grandmother made a worse match.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. My lord of Gloucester, I have borne your blunt reproaches and bitter jeers too long. By heaven, I will tell his Majesty about these gross insults that I have often endured. I would rather be a country servant-girl than a great queen on these terms, to be so baited, scorned and raged at.
Enter old Queen Margaret behind.
I have little joy in being England's queen.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside._] And may that little be lessened, I beg God!
Your honor, rank and throne are owed to me.

RICHARD. What, do you threaten me with telling the King? Tell him, and don't hold back. I will stand by whatever I have said in the King's presence. I dare risk being sent to the Tower. It is time to speak out. My labors are quite forgotten.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside._] Out, devil! I remember them too well.
You killed my husband Henry in the Tower, and Edward, my poor son, at Tewksbury.

RICHARD. Before you were queen, yes, or your husband king, I was a pack-horse in his great affairs, a weeder-out of his proud enemies and a generous rewarder of his friends. To make his blood royal, I spilled my own.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside._] Yes, and much better blood than his or yours.

RICHARD. In all that time, you and your husband Grey were partisans of the house of Lancaster. And, Rivers, so were you. Was your husband not killed in Margaret's battle at Saint Albans? Let me remind you, in case you forget, what you were before this and what you are now, and also what I was and what I am.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside._] A murderous villain, and so you still are.
RICHARD. Poor Clarence abandoned his father-in-law Warwick, yes, and broke his oath, which Jesus pardon!
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside._] Which God avenge!

RICHARD. To fight on Edward's side for the crown. And for his reward, poor lord, he is shut up in prison. I wish to God my heart were flint, like Edward's, or Edward's soft and pitying, like mine. I am too childishly foolish for this world.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside._] Hurry to hell, for shame, and leave this world,
you evil spirit! Your kingdom is there.
RIVERS. My lord of Gloucester, in those busy days which you bring up here to prove us enemies, we followed our lord, our sovereign king. So we would follow you, if you should be our king.
RICHARD. If I should be! I would rather be a peddler. Far be the thought of it from my heart.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. My lord, you suppose you would have as little joy as I would, were you king of this country. You may suppose, then, that I have just as little joy in being its Queen.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside._] The Queen of this country has as little joy,
for I am she, and altogether joyless. I can no longer hold my patience.
[_Coming forward._]

Hear me, you quarreling pirates, who fall out over dividing what you have plundered from me! Which of you does not tremble when he looks at me? If you don't bow to me as your Queen, you quake like rebels because you deposed me. Ah, gentle villain, do not turn away.
RICHARD. Foul, wrinkled witch, what are you doing in my sight?
QUEEN MARGARET. Only repeating what you have ruined. I will do that before I let you go.
RICHARD. Weren't you banished on pain of death?

QUEEN MARGARET. I was. But I find more pain in banishment than death could give me by my staying here. You owe me a husband and a son. You owe me a kingdom. All of you owe me allegiance. The sorrow I have is by right yours, and all the pleasures you have usurped are mine.

RICHARD. The curse that my noble father laid on you when you crowned his warlike brows with paper, and with your scorn drew rivers from his eyes, and then, to dry them, gave the Duke a rag soaked in the innocent blood of pretty Rutland, those curses, spoken then from the bitterness of his soul against you, have all fallen on you. And God, not we, has punished your bloody deed.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. God is so just, to defend the innocent.
HASTINGS. Oh, it was the foulest deed, to slay that child, and the most merciless ever heard of.
RIVERS. Even tyrants wept when it was reported.
DORSET. No man failed to prophesy revenge for it.
BUCKINGHAM. Northumberland, who was there, wept to see it.

QUEEN MARGARET. What, were you all snarling before I came, ready to catch each other by the throat, and now you turn all your hatred on me? Did York's dread curse prevail so much with heaven that Henry's death, my lovely Edward's death, the loss of their kingdom and my woeful banishment should all pay only for that peevish brat? Can curses pierce the clouds and enter heaven? Why then, make way, dull clouds, for my swift curses! Though not by war, may your King die of overindulgence, as our King died by murder, to make him a king. May Edward your son, who is now Prince of Wales, die young by a like untimely violence, for Edward our son, who was Prince of Wales. May you, a queen, outlive your glory, as I, who was a queen, have done, wretched as I am. Long may you live to wail your children's death, and see another woman, as I see you now, dressed in your rights, as you are seated in mine. May your happy days die long before your death, and after many long hours of grief, may you die neither mother, wife nor England's Queen. Rivers and Dorset, you were standing by, and so were you, Lord Hastings, when my son was stabbed with bloody daggers. God, I pray, may none of you live out your natural age, but be cut off by some unexpected accident.
RICHARD. Have done with your spell, you hateful withered hag.

QUEEN MARGARET. Leave you out? No, stay, dog, because you will hear me. If heaven has any worse plague in store than the ones I can wish on you, oh, let it hold that plague back until your sins are ripe. Then let heaven hurl its anger down on you, the man who troubles the peace of this poor world. May the worm of conscience gnaw at your soul forever. While you live, may you suspect your friends of treason, and take deep traitors for your dearest friends. May no sleep ever close that deadly eye of yours, except when some tormenting dream terrifies you with a hell full of ugly devils. You elf-marked, misbegotten, rooting hog! You were stamped at your birth as nature's slave and hell's son. You are a slander on your sorrowing mother's womb. You are the loathed offspring of your father's loins. You rag of honor, you detested—
RICHARD. Margaret.
QUEEN MARGARET. Richard!
RICHARD. Ha?
QUEEN MARGARET. I am not calling you.
RICHARD. Then I beg your pardon. I thought you had called me all those bitter names.
QUEEN MARGARET. Why, so I did, but I expected no answer. Oh, let me finish my curse!
RICHARD. I have finished it for you, and it ends in "Margaret".
QUEEN ELIZABETH. So you have cursed yourself.

QUEEN MARGARET. Poor painted queen, you empty show of what my fortune used to be! Why do you sprinkle sugar on that bloated spider, whose deadly web is trapping you all around? Fool, fool! You are sharpening a knife to kill yourself. The day will come when you will wish I were here to help you curse this poisonous hunchbacked toad.
HASTINGS. You false-prophesying woman, end your frantic curse, or you will push our patience too far, to your own harm.
QUEEN MARGARET. Shame on you all, you have already pushed mine too far.
RIVERS. If you were treated as you deserve, you would be taught your duty.

QUEEN MARGARET. To treat me as I deserve, you should all do your duty to me. You should learn to treat me as your queen, and yourselves as my subjects. Oh, treat me as I deserve, and teach yourselves that duty!
DORSET. Don't argue with her. She is a lunatic.

QUEEN MARGARET. Quiet, Master Marquess, you are impudent. Your brand-new stamp of honor is hardly valid currency yet. Oh, I wish your young nobility could understand what it is to lose it and be wretched! Those who stand high have many gusts to shake them, and if they fall they smash themselves to pieces.
RICHARD. Good advice, indeed. Learn it, learn it, Marquess.
DORSET. It concerns you, my lord, as much as me.
RICHARD. Yes, and much more, but I was born so high. Our eagle's nest is built in the top of the cedar. It plays with the wind and scorns the sun.

QUEEN MARGARET. And turns the sun into shade, alas, alas! Witness my son, who now lies in the shadow of death. Your cloudy anger wrapped his bright shining beams in eternal darkness. Your eagle's nest is built in our eagle's nest. O God, who sees it, do not let it go on! As it was won with blood, let it be lost the same way.
BUCKINGHAM. Quiet, quiet, for shame, if not out of charity.

QUEEN MARGARET. Do not speak to me of charity or shame. You have dealt with me without charity, and you have shamefully butchered my hopes. My charity is rage, my life is shame, and in that shame my sorrow's rage lives on.
BUCKINGHAM. Enough, enough.

QUEEN MARGARET. Oh, princely Buckingham, I'll kiss your hand as a sign of alliance and friendship with you. May good fortune come to you and your noble house! Your clothes are not stained with our blood, and you are not within the reach of my curse.
BUCKINGHAM. Nor is anyone here, because curses never get past the lips of those who breathe them into the air.

QUEEN MARGARET. I cannot help thinking they rise to the sky and wake God's gentle, sleeping peace. Oh, Buckingham, watch out for that dog over there! See how he bites when he fawns, and when he bites, his venomous tooth festers until death. Have nothing to do with him. Beware of him. Sin, death and hell have marked him, and all their servants attend him.
RICHARD. What is she saying, my lord of Buckingham?
BUCKINGHAM. Nothing I care about, my gracious lord.

QUEEN MARGARET. What, do you scorn me for my kind advice, and flatter the devil I am warning you against? Oh, but remember this some other day, when he splits your very heart with sorrow, and you say, poor Margaret was a prophetess. Each of you, live as the subject of his hate, and he of yours, and all of you of God's!
[_Exit._]
BUCKINGHAM. My hair stands on end to hear her curses.
RIVERS. So does mine. I wonder why she is free.
RICHARD. I cannot blame her. By God's holy mother, she has suffered too much wrong, and I regret the part I played in it.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. To my knowledge, I never wronged her at all.

RICHARD. Yet you all profit from the wrong done to her. I was too eager to help someone who is too cold now to think of it. Why, as for Clarence, he is well repaid: he is shut up in a pen, being fattened for his pains. God forgive those who are the cause of it.
RIVERS. A virtuous and Christian conclusion, to pray for those who have harmed us.
RICHARD. So I always do—(_Speaks to himself_) when I am well advised. For if I had cursed just now, I would have cursed myself.
Enter Catesby.
CATESBY. Madam, His Majesty is calling for you, and for your Grace, and for you, my gracious lords.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Catesby, I'm coming. Lords, will you go with me?
RIVERS. We attend your Grace.
[_Exeunt all but Richard._]

RICHARD. I do the wrong, and I am the first to start the quarrel. The secret evils I set going, I lay as a heavy charge on other people. Clarence, whom I myself have thrown into darkness, I weep for in front of many simple fools, namely Derby, Hastings and Buckingham. I tell them it is the Queen and her allies who stir the King up against my brother the Duke. Now they believe it, and on top of that they urge me to take revenge on Rivers, Dorset and Grey. But then I sigh, and with a piece of Scripture I tell them that God commands us to return good for evil. And so I clothe my naked villainy with odd old scraps stolen from Holy Writ, and seem a saint when I am most playing the devil.
Enter two Murderers.
But quiet, here come my executioners. Well, my bold, stout, determined fellows, are you on your way now to finish this business?
FIRST MURDERER. We are, my lord, and we have come to get the warrant, so that we can be let in where he is.
RICHARD. Well thought of. I have it here on me.
[_Gives the warrant._]

When you have done it, come to Crosby Place. But, gentlemen, be quick about the execution, and be hard-hearted, don't listen to him plead. For Clarence is a good talker, and if you listen to him he may perhaps move your hearts to pity.
SECOND MURDERER. Tut, tut, my lord, we will not stand around chattering. Talkers are no good at doing. Be assured, we are going to use our hands and not our tongues.
RICHARD. Your eyes drop millstones where fools' eyes shed tears. I like you, lads. Get to your business right away. Go, go, finish it.
BOTH MURDERERS. We will, my noble lord.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — London. A Room in the Tower
paragraphs: Enter Clarence and Keeper.
KEEPER. Why does your Grace look so heavy today?

CLARENCE. Oh, I have spent a miserable night, so full of fearful dreams and ugly sights that, as I am a faithful Christian, I would not spend another night like it, even to buy a world of happy days. The time was so full of dismal terror!
KEEPER. What was your dream, my lord? Please tell me.

CLARENCE. I thought I had broken out of the Tower and was sailing across to Burgundy. My brother Gloucester was with me, and he coaxed me out of my cabin to walk on the deck. From there we looked toward England, and we recalled a thousand sad times that had befallen us during the wars of York and Lancaster. As we paced along the unsteady footing of the deck, I thought Gloucester stumbled. As he fell, he struck me, who was trying to hold him back, and knocked me overboard into the tumbling waves of the sea. O Lord, how painful it seemed to drown! What a dreadful noise of waters in my ears, what sights of ugly death before my eyes! I thought I saw a thousand fearful shipwrecks, a thousand men that fishes had gnawed on, wedges of gold, great anchors, heaps of pearl, priceless stones and jewels beyond value, all scattered on the bottom of the sea. Some lay in dead men's skulls. In the holes where eyes once lived, jewels had crept in, as if in scorn of eyes. They glittered, courting the slimy bottom of the deep and mocking the dead bones scattered beside them.
KEEPER. Did you have time, while you were dying, to gaze at these secrets of the deep?

CLARENCE. I thought I did. Often I struggled to give up the ghost, but the envious water kept my soul stopped inside me. It would not let it go out to find the empty, vast, wandering air. It smothered the soul inside my panting body, which almost burst trying to breathe it out into the sea.
KEEPER. Didn't you wake in this terrible agony?

CLARENCE. No, no, my dream went on after death. Oh, then the storm began in my soul. I thought I crossed the gloomy river with that sour ferryman the poets write about, to the kingdom of everlasting night. The first to greet my stranger-soul there was my great father-in-law, the famous Warwick. He cried out loud, "What punishment for perjury can this dark kingdom offer false Clarence?" And then he vanished. Next came wandering by a shadow like an angel, with bright hair soaked in blood. He shrieked out loud, "Clarence has come, false, fickle, perjured Clarence, who stabbed me in the field at Tewksbury! Seize him, Furies! Take him away to torment!" At that, I thought, a legion of foul fiends surrounded me and howled in my ears such hideous cries that the very noise woke me, trembling. For some time afterward I could not believe I was anywhere but in hell, so terrible was the impression my dream made.
KEEPER. No wonder it frightened you, my lord. I am afraid myself, I think, just hearing you tell it.

CLARENCE. Ah, Keeper, Keeper, I have done these things that now bear witness against my soul, and I did them for Edward's sake. And see how he repays me! O God, if my deep prayers cannot appease you, and you must be avenged for my misdeeds, then carry out your wrath on me alone. Oh, spare my innocent wife and my poor children! Keeper, please sit by me for a while. My soul is heavy, and I would gladly sleep.
KEEPER. I will, my lord. God give your Grace good rest.
[_Clarence reposes himself on a chair._]
Enter Brakenbury the Lieutenant.

BRAKENBURY. Sorrow breaks up seasons and hours of rest. It makes the night morning and the noon night. Princes have only their titles for their glory, an outward honor for an inward toil. And for imaginings they never feel, they often feel a world of restless cares. So between their titles and a lowly name there is no difference but outward fame.
Enter the two Murderers.
FIRST MURDERER. Ho, who's here?
BRAKENBURY. What do you want, fellow? And how did you get here?
SECOND MURDERER. I want to speak with Clarence, and I got here on my legs.
BRAKENBURY. What, so short?
FIRST MURDERER. It's better, sir, than being long-winded. Let him see our commission, and say no more.
[_Brakenbury reads the commission._]

BRAKENBURY. By this I am commanded to hand the noble Duke of Clarence over to you. I will not ask what is meant by it, because I want to be innocent of its meaning. There lies the Duke asleep, and here are the keys. I'll go to the King and tell him that I have given up my charge to you.
FIRST MURDERER. You may, sir. It's a wise move. Goodbye.
[_Exeunt Brakenbury and the Keeper._]
SECOND MURDERER. What, shall I stab him while he sleeps?
FIRST MURDERER. No. When he wakes he'll say it was done cowardly.
SECOND MURDERER. Why, he will never wake until the great Judgement Day.
FIRST MURDERER. Why, then he'll say we stabbed him in his sleep.
SECOND MURDERER. Bringing up that word "judgement" has bred a kind of remorse in me.
FIRST MURDERER. What, are you afraid?
SECOND MURDERER. Not of killing him, since I have a warrant. But of being damned for killing him, and no warrant can protect me from that.
FIRST MURDERER. I thought you were resolved.
SECOND MURDERER. So I am: to let him live.
FIRST MURDERER. I'll go back to the Duke of Gloucester and tell him so.
SECOND MURDERER. No, please, wait a little. I hope this emotional mood will pass. It used to last only as long as it takes to count to twenty.
FIRST MURDERER. How do you feel now?
SECOND MURDERER. Faith, there are still some leftover dregs of conscience in me.
FIRST MURDERER. Remember our reward when the deed is done.
SECOND MURDERER. Damn it, he dies! I had forgotten the reward.
FIRST MURDERER. Where's your conscience now?
SECOND MURDERER. Oh, in the Duke of Gloucester's purse.
FIRST MURDERER. So when he opens his purse to give us our reward, your conscience flies out.
SECOND MURDERER. It doesn't matter. Let it go. Few or none will take it in.
FIRST MURDERER. What if it comes back to you?

SECOND MURDERER. I won't have anything to do with it. It makes a man a coward. A man can't steal without it accusing him. He can't swear without it stopping him. He can't sleep with his neighbor's wife without it exposing him. It is a blushing, shamefaced spirit that rebels in a man's chest. It fills a man full of obstacles. It once made me give back a purse of gold I found by chance. It makes a beggar of any man who keeps it. It is driven out of towns and cities as a dangerous thing, and every man who means to live well tries to rely on himself and live without it.
FIRST MURDERER. Damn it, it's at my elbow right now, persuading me not to kill the Duke.
SECOND MURDERER. Take the devil into your mind and don't believe it. It would creep up on you just to make you sigh.
FIRST MURDERER. I'm strongly built. It can't win me over.
SECOND MURDERER. Spoken like a brave man who cares about his reputation. Come, shall we get to work?
FIRST MURDERER. Hit him on the head with the hilt of your sword, and then throw him in the barrel of malmsey wine in the next room.
SECOND MURDERER. Oh, excellent plan, and make a soaked bread-sop of him.
FIRST MURDERER. Quiet, he's waking.
SECOND MURDERER. Strike!
FIRST MURDERER. No, we'll talk with him first.
CLARENCE. Where are you, keeper? Give me a cup of wine.
SECOND MURDERER. You shall have wine enough, my lord, soon.
CLARENCE. In God's name, what are you?
FIRST MURDERER. A man, as you are.
CLARENCE. But not as I am, royal.
SECOND MURDERER. And you are not as we are, loyal.
CLARENCE. Your voice is thunder, but your looks are humble.
FIRST MURDERER. My voice is now the King's, my looks are my own.
CLARENCE. How dark and deadly you speak! Your eyes threaten me. Why do you look pale? Who sent you here? Why have you come?
SECOND MURDERER. To, to, to—
CLARENCE. To murder me?
BOTH MURDERERS. Yes, yes.
CLARENCE. You hardly have the hearts to tell me so, and therefore you cannot have the hearts to do it. How, my friends, have I offended you?
FIRST MURDERER. You have not offended us, but you have offended the King.
CLARENCE. I shall be reconciled with him again.
SECOND MURDERER. Never, my lord. So prepare to die.

CLARENCE. Have you been picked out from among all men to kill the innocent? What is my offense? Where is the evidence that accuses me? What lawful jury has handed its verdict up to the frowning judge? Or who pronounced the bitter sentence of poor Clarence's death? Before I am convicted by due course of law, it is most unlawful to threaten me with death. I charge you, as you hope for redemption through Christ's dear blood shed for our grievous sins, to go away and lay no hands on me. The deed you are undertaking is damnable.
FIRST MURDERER. What we will do, we do on orders.
SECOND MURDERER. And the one who gave the orders is our King.

CLARENCE. You mistaken servants! The great King of kings has commanded in the tablets of his law, "You shall not murder." Will you then spurn his command and carry out a man's? Take care, for he holds vengeance in his hand, ready to hurl it on the heads of those who break his law.
SECOND MURDERER. And he hurls that same vengeance on you, for false oath-breaking, and for murder too. You took the sacrament to fight on behalf of the house of Lancaster.
FIRST MURDERER. And like a traitor to the name of God, you broke that vow. With your treacherous blade you ripped open the belly of your sovereign's son.
SECOND MURDERER. The man you had sworn to cherish and defend.
FIRST MURDERER. How can you quote God's dreadful law to us, when you have broken it so badly yourself?

CLARENCE. Alas, for whose sake did I do that evil deed? For Edward, for my brother, for his sake. He does not send you to murder me for it, because in that sin he is as deep as I am. If God will be avenged for the deed, oh, know that he does it openly. Do not take the quarrel out of his powerful arm. He needs no roundabout or lawless means to cut off those who have offended him.
FIRST MURDERER. Then who made you a bloody agent of death when the gallant, spirited, brave Plantagenet, that princely newcomer to war, was struck dead by you?
CLARENCE. My brother's love, the devil, and my rage.
FIRST MURDERER. Your brother's love, our duty, and your faults bring us here now to slaughter you.

CLARENCE. If you love my brother, do not hate me. I am his brother, and I love him well. If you are hired for pay, go back, and I will send you to my brother Gloucester. He will reward you better for my life than Edward will for news of my death.
SECOND MURDERER. You are mistaken. Your brother Gloucester hates you.
CLARENCE. Oh no, he loves me and holds me dear. Go to him from me.
FIRST MURDERER. Yes, so we will.

CLARENCE. Tell him that when our princely father York blessed his three sons with his victorious arm, and charged us from his soul to love each other, he little thought of this divided friendship. Tell Gloucester to think of this, and he will weep.
FIRST MURDERER. Yes, millstones, as he taught us to weep.
CLARENCE. Oh, do not slander him, for he is kind.
FIRST MURDERER. Right, as snow in harvest time. Come, you deceive yourself. He is the one who sends us to destroy you here.
CLARENCE. It cannot be, because he wept over my misfortune, hugged me in his arms, and swore with sobs that he would work to get me released.
FIRST MURDERER. Why, so he is doing, when he releases you from the bondage of this earth to the joys of heaven.
SECOND MURDERER. Make your peace with God, for you must die, my lord.

CLARENCE. Do you have that holy feeling in your souls, to advise me to make my peace with God, and yet are you so blind to your own souls that you will make war on God by murdering me? Oh, sirs, consider this: those who set you on to do this deed will hate you for the deed.
SECOND MURDERER. What shall we do?
CLARENCE. Relent, and save your souls.
FIRST MURDERER. Relent? No, that's cowardly and womanish.

CLARENCE. Not to relent is beastly, savage and devilish. Which of you, if you were a prince's son shut off from freedom as I am now, and two murderers like yourselves came to you, would not plead for his life? Yes, you would beg, if you were in my distress. My friend, I see some pity in your looks. Oh, if your eye is not a flatterer, come over to my side and plead for me. What beggar does not pity a begging prince?
SECOND MURDERER. Look behind you, my lord.
FIRST MURDERER. Take that, and that! [_Stabs him._] If all this will not do, I'll drown you in the barrel of malmsey inside.
[_Exit with the body._]
SECOND MURDERER. A bloody deed, and desperately done. How gladly would I, like Pilate, wash my hands of this most grievous murder.
Enter First Murderer.
FIRST MURDERER. What now? What do you mean by not helping me? By heaven, the Duke will hear how slack you have been.
SECOND MURDERER. I wish he knew that I had saved his brother. Take the fee yourself, and tell him what I say, because I regret that the Duke is dead.
[_Exit._]

FIRST MURDERER. I don't. Go, coward that you are. Well, I'll go hide the body in some hole until the Duke gives orders for his burial. And when I have my pay, I'll be off, for this will come out, and then I must not stay around.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — London. A Room in the palace
paragraphs: Enter King Edward, sick, Queen Elizabeth, Dorset, Rivers, Hastings, Buckingham, Grey and others.

KING EDWARD. Well, so. Now I have done a good day's work. You peers, keep up this united league. Every day I expect a message from my Redeemer to take me away from here. My soul will leave for heaven more at peace, since I have made my friends be at peace on earth. Rivers and Hastings, take each other's hand. Do not hide your hatred. Swear your love.
RIVERS. By heaven, my soul is cleansed of grudging hate, and with my hand I seal my true heart's love.
HASTINGS. May I prosper only as I truly swear the same.
KING EDWARD. Take care you do not play games in front of your King, or He who is the supreme King of kings will destroy your hidden falsehood and make each of you the other's death.
HASTINGS. May I prosper only as I swear perfect love.
RIVERS. And I, as I love Hastings with my heart.

KING EDWARD. Madam, you yourself are not exempt from this, nor you, son Dorset, nor you, Buckingham. You have been quarreling with one another. Wife, love Lord Hastings, let him kiss your hand, and whatever you do, do it sincerely.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. There, Hastings, I will never again remember our former hatred, so may I and mine prosper.
KING EDWARD. Dorset, embrace him. Hastings, love the Lord Marquess.
DORSET. I declare here that this exchange of love will be unbroken on my part.
HASTINGS. And so I swear.
[_They embrace._]
KING EDWARD. Now, princely Buckingham, seal this league by embracing my wife's allies, and make me happy in your unity.

BUCKINGHAM. If Buckingham ever turns his hate on your Grace, instead of cherishing you and yours with all dutiful love, may God punish me by making those I expect most love from hate me. When I most need a friend, and am most sure he is a friend, may he be deep, hollow, treacherous and full of deceit toward me. This I beg of God, if I am ever cold in love to you or yours.
[_Embrace._]
KING EDWARD. This vow of yours, princely Buckingham, is a pleasing cordial to my sickly heart. All we lack now is our brother Gloucester here, to make the blessed end of this peace.
BUCKINGHAM. And in good time, here comes Sir Ratcliffe and the Duke.
Enter Ratcliffe and Richard.
RICHARD. Good morning to my sovereign King and Queen, and, princely peers, a happy time of day to you.

KING EDWARD. Happy indeed, considering how we have spent the day. Gloucester, we have done deeds of charity. We have made peace out of enmity and fair love out of hate between these swollen, wrongfully angered peers.

RICHARD. A blessed labor, my most sovereign lord, among this princely crowd. If anyone here, through false information or wrong suspicion, takes me for an enemy, or if I have unwittingly, or in my anger, done anything that anyone in this company finds hard to bear, I want to be reconciled and have his friendly peace. Being at enmity is death to me. I hate it, and I want the love of all good men. First, madam, I ask for true peace from you, which I will earn with my dutiful service. From you, my noble cousin Buckingham, if ever any grudge lodged between us. From you and you, Lord Rivers and Dorset, who have frowned on me without any cause. From you, Lord Woodville and Lord Scales. From you, dukes, earls, lords, gentlemen: indeed, from all. I know of no Englishman alive with whom my soul is at odds in the least, any more than the infant who is born tonight. I thank my God for my humility.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. This will be kept as a holy day from now on. I wish to God all quarrels were well settled. My sovereign lord, I beg your Highness to take our brother Clarence back into your favor.
RICHARD. Why, madam, have I offered love only to be mocked like this in the royal presence? Who does not know that the gentle Duke is dead?
[_They all start._]
You do him an injury to scorn his corpse.
KING EDWARD. Who does not know he is dead! Who knows he is?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. All-seeing heaven, what a world this is!
BUCKINGHAM. Do I look as pale, Lord Dorset, as the rest?
DORSET. Yes, my good lord, and there is no man in the room whose red color has not left his cheeks.
KING EDWARD. Is Clarence dead? The order was canceled.

RICHARD. But he, poor man, died by your first order, which a winged Mercury carried. Some slow cripple carried the cancellation, which came too late to see him buried. God grant that some men who are less noble and less loyal, and closer in bloody thoughts though not in blood, do not deserve worse than wretched Clarence did, and yet pass without suspicion!
Enter Stanley Earl of Derby.
STANLEY. A favor, my sovereign, for my service done!
KING EDWARD. Please, quiet. My soul is full of sorrow.
STANLEY. I will not rise unless your Highness hears me.
KING EDWARD. Then say at once what it is you ask.
STANLEY. The pardon, sovereign, of my servant's life. He killed a riotous gentleman today, who lately served the Duke of Norfolk.

KING EDWARD. Have I a tongue that pronounced my brother's death, and shall that same tongue pardon a servant? My brother killed no man. His fault was a thought, and yet his punishment was bitter death. Who pleaded with me for him? Who, in my wrath, knelt at my feet and told me to think it over? Who spoke of brotherhood? Who spoke of love? Who told me how the poor soul abandoned the mighty Warwick and fought for me? Who told me, in the field at Tewksbury, when Oxford had me down, that he rescued me and said, "Dear brother, live, and be a king"? Who told me, when we both lay in the field frozen almost to death, how he wrapped me in his own clothes and gave himself, thin and naked, to the numbing cold night? Brutish wrath sinfully plucked all of this out of my memory, and not one of you had enough grace to put it back in my mind. But when your carters or your serving men have done a drunken killing and defaced the precious image of our dear Redeemer, you are straight away on your knees for pardon, pardon, and I, unjustly too, must grant it to you. But for my brother not one man would speak, nor did I, ungracious, speak to myself for him, poor soul. The proudest of you all were indebted to him in his life, yet not one of you would once beg for his life. Oh God, I fear your justice will take hold of me, and of you, and of mine and yours for this! Come, Hastings, help me to my private room. Ah, poor Clarence!
[_Exeunt some with King and Queen._]

RICHARD. This is the fruit of rashness. Didn't you notice how the guilty kindred of the Queen looked pale when they heard of Clarence's death? Oh, they kept urging it on the King. God will take revenge for it. Come, lords, will you go to comfort Edward with our company?
BUCKINGHAM. We attend your Grace.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Another Room in the palace
paragraphs: Enter the old Duchess of York with the two Children of Clarence.
BOY. Good grandma, tell us, is our father dead?
DUCHESS. No, boy.
GIRL. Why do you weep so often and beat your breast, and cry "Oh Clarence, my unhappy son"?
BOY. Why do you look at us and shake your head, and call us orphans, wretches, castaways, if our noble father is alive?

DUCHESS. My pretty grandchildren, you are both mistaken. I am mourning the King's sickness, because I am reluctant to lose him, not your father's death. It would be wasted sorrow to cry over someone who is already lost.
BOY. Then you are saying, grandma, that he is dead. The King, my uncle, is to blame for it. God will take revenge for it, and I will pester him with earnest prayers to that end.
GIRL. And so will I.
DUCHESS. Quiet, children, quiet. The King loves you well. You innocent little ones, too young and shallow to understand, you cannot guess who caused your father's death.

BOY. Grandma, we can, because my good uncle Gloucester told me that the King, provoked to it by the Queen, devised accusations to imprison him. And when my uncle told me so, he wept, and pitied me, and kindly kissed my cheek. He told me to rely on him as on my father, and said he would love me dearly as his child.
DUCHESS. Ah, that deceit should steal such a gentle shape, and hide deep vice behind a virtuous mask! He is my son, yes, and that is my shame. Yet he did not draw this deceit from my breast.
BOY. Do you think my uncle was pretending, grandma?
DUCHESS. Yes, boy.
BOY. I cannot think it. Listen, what is that noise?
Enter Queen Elizabeth with her hair about her ears, Rivers and Dorset after her.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, who will stop me from wailing and weeping, from scolding my fortune and tormenting myself? I'll join forces with black despair against my own soul and become my own enemy.
DUCHESS. What does this scene of wild impatience mean?

QUEEN ELIZABETH. It means an act of tragic violence. Edward, my lord, your son, our King, is dead. Why do the branches grow when the root is gone? Why do the leaves that lack their sap not wither? If you want to live, lament. If you want to die, be quick, so that our swift-winged souls may catch up with the King's, or like obedient subjects follow him to his new kingdom of never-changing night.

DUCHESS. Ah, I have as much stake in your sorrow as I had claim to your noble husband. I wept for the death of a worthy husband, and lived by looking at his images. But now two mirrors of his princely likeness have been cracked in pieces by malignant death, and for comfort I have only one false glass, which grieves me when I see my shame in him. You are a widow, yet you are a mother, and you have the comfort of your children left. But death has snatched my husband from my arms and plucked two crutches from my feeble hands, Clarence and Edward. Oh, what cause I have, since yours is only half my grief, to outdo your woes and drown out your cries.
BOY. Ah, aunt, you did not weep for our father's death. How can we help you with our kindred tears?
GIRL. Our fatherless distress was left unmourned. May your widow's grief likewise go unwept!

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Give me no help in lamenting. I am not barren when it comes to producing complaints. All springs send their streams to my eyes, so that, ruled by the watery moon, I may pour out plenty of tears to drown the world. Ah, for my husband, for my dear Lord Edward!
CHILDREN. Ah for our father, for our dear Lord Clarence!
DUCHESS. Alas for both, both mine, Edward and Clarence!
QUEEN ELIZABETH. What support had I but Edward? And he is gone.
CHILDREN. What support had we but Clarence? And he is gone.
DUCHESS. What supports had I but them? And they are gone.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. No widow ever had so dear a loss.
CHILDREN. No orphans ever had so dear a loss.

DUCHESS. No mother ever had so dear a loss. Alas, I am the mother of all these griefs. Their woes are divided up, mine is the whole. She weeps for an Edward, and so do I. I weep for a Clarence, and she does not. These babes weep for Clarence, and so do I. I weep for an Edward, and they do not. Alas, you three, pour all your tears on me, who am threefold distressed. I am your sorrow's nurse, and I will feed it with lamentation.

DORSET. Take comfort, dear mother. God is greatly displeased that you take his doing with ingratitude. In ordinary worldly matters it is called ungrateful to repay a debt grudgingly and reluctantly when it was kindly lent with a generous hand. It is much worse to be so opposed to heaven, which asks back the royal debt it lent you.

RIVERS. Madam, think, like a careful mother, of the young prince your son. Send for him at once. Let him be crowned. Your comfort lives in him. Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward's grave, and plant your joys on living Edward's throne.
Enter Richard, Buckingham, Stanley Earl of Derby, Hastings and Ratcliffe.

RICHARD. Sister, take comfort. All of us have cause to wail the dimming of our shining star, but nobody can mend our harms by wailing over them. Madam my mother, I beg your pardon. I did not see your Grace. Humbly on my knee I ask for your blessing.
[_Kneels._]
DUCHESS. God bless you, and put meekness in your breast, love, charity, obedience and true duty.
RICHARD. Amen. [_Aside_.] And make me die a good old man! That is the tail end of a mother's blessing. I wonder that her Grace left it out.

BUCKINGHAM. You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers who bear this heavy shared load of grief, now cheer each other with each other's love. Though we have used up our harvest from this king, we are to reap the harvest of his son. The broken-off rancor of your high-swollen hatreds, only lately mended, knit and joined together, must be gently preserved, cherished and kept. It seems good to me that with only a small escort the young Prince be fetched from Ludlow here to London, to be crowned our King.
RIVERS. Why with only a small escort, my Lord of Buckingham?

BUCKINGHAM. Why, my lord, so that a crowd does not make the newly healed wound of malice break out again. That would be all the more dangerous the more the state is young and not yet governed. Where every horse wears his own commanding rein and can steer his course as he pleases, I think the fear of harm, as well as harm in plain sight, ought to be prevented.
RICHARD. I hope the King made peace with all of us, and the pact is firm and true in me.

RIVERS. And so in me, and so, I think, in all. Yet since it is still new, it should not be exposed to any visible chance of a breach, which a large company might perhaps provoke. Therefore I agree with noble Buckingham that it is fitting that so few should fetch the Prince.
HASTINGS. And so say I.
RICHARD. Then so be it, and let us go decide who shall ride straight to Ludlow. Madam, and you, my sister, will you come to give your opinions in this business?
[_Exeunt all but Buckingham and Richard._]

BUCKINGHAM. My lord, whoever travels to the Prince, for God's sake, let us two not stay at home. For on the way I'll find an occasion, as a start to the story we recently talked about, to separate the Queen's proud kindred from the Prince.
RICHARD. My other self, the council chamber of my counsels, my oracle, my prophet, my dear cousin, I will go by your direction like a child. Toward Ludlow, then, for we will not stay behind.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — London. A street
paragraphs: Enter one Citizen at one door, and Another at the other.
FIRST CITIZEN. Good morning, neighbor. Where are you off to in such a hurry?
SECOND CITIZEN. To tell you the truth, I hardly know myself. Have you heard the news going around?
FIRST CITIZEN. Yes, that the King is dead.
SECOND CITIZEN. Bad news, by Our Lady. Better news rarely follows it. I fear, I fear this will turn into a world gone wild.
Enter another Citizen.
THIRD CITIZEN. Neighbors, God be with you.
FIRST CITIZEN. Good morning to you, sir.
THIRD CITIZEN. Is it true, then, that good King Edward is dead?
SECOND CITIZEN. Yes, sir, it's too true. God help us now.
THIRD CITIZEN. Then, gentlemen, expect troubled times.
FIRST CITIZEN. No, no. By God's good grace, his son will reign.
THIRD CITIZEN. Pity the country that's governed by a child.

SECOND CITIZEN. There is hope that he will govern well. While he's a minor, a council will govern under him. When he's fully grown, he will govern himself. I have no doubt he will govern well, both then and until then.
FIRST CITIZEN. That's how things stood when Henry the Sixth was crowned in Paris at only nine months old.

THIRD CITIZEN. Is that how things stood? No, no, good friends, God knows they didn't. Back then this country was famously enriched with wise and serious counsel. The King had virtuous uncles to protect him.
FIRST CITIZEN. Well, so does this one, on both his father's side and his mother's.

THIRD CITIZEN. It would be better if they all came from his father's side, or if none did. Now they'll compete over who stands nearest the throne, and that rivalry will hit us all too hard, unless God prevents it. Oh, the Duke of Gloucester is full of danger, and the Queen's sons and brothers are haughty and proud. If they were made to obey instead of rule, this sick country might find comfort as it did before.
FIRST CITIZEN. Come, come, we're fearing the worst. All will be well.

THIRD CITIZEN. When clouds appear, wise men put on their cloaks. When the great leaves fall, winter is near. When the sun sets, who doesn't expect night? Storms out of season make men expect famine. All may be well. But if God arranges it so, that's more than we deserve or I expect.
SECOND CITIZEN. Truly, people's hearts are full of fear. You can hardly talk with a man who doesn't look gloomy and full of dread.

THIRD CITIZEN. It's always like this before times of change. By a divine instinct, people's minds sense the danger ahead, just as we see the water swell before a violent storm. But leave it all to God. Where are you headed?
SECOND CITIZEN. Why, we've been sent for by the Justices.
THIRD CITIZEN. So have I. I'll keep you company.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — London. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: Enter the Archbishop of York, the young Duke of York, Queen Elizabeth and the Duchess of York.
ARCHBISHOP. Last night, I hear, they stayed at Stony Stratford, and tonight they rest at Northampton. Tomorrow or the next day they will be here.
DUCHESS. I long with all my heart to see the Prince. I hope he has grown a lot since I last saw him.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But I hear not. They say my son York has almost caught up with him in height.
YORK. Yes, mother, but I wish it weren't so.
DUCHESS. Why, my good grandson? It's good to grow.

YORK. Grandmother, one night as we sat at supper, my uncle Rivers said I was growing more than my brother. "Yes," said my uncle Gloucester, "small herbs have grace; great weeds grow fast." Since then I think I'd rather not grow so fast, because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.

DUCHESS. Honestly, honestly, that saying didn't hold true for the man who threw it at you! When he was young he was the most wretched creature, so slow and leisurely in growing that if his own rule were true, he would be full of grace.
ARCHBISHOP. And so, no doubt, he is, my gracious lady.
DUCHESS. I hope he is. But still, let mothers doubt.
YORK. Now, upon my word, if I had remembered, I could have thrown a jibe at my uncle's Grace that hit his growth closer than he hit mine.
DUCHESS. How, my young York? Please, let me hear it.
YORK. Why, they say my uncle grew so fast that he could gnaw a crust at two hours old. It was a full two years before I got a tooth. Grandmother, this would have been a biting joke.
DUCHESS. Please, pretty York, who told you this?
YORK. His nurse, Grandmother.
DUCHESS. His nurse? Why, she was dead before you were born.
YORK. If it wasn't her, I can't tell who told me.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. A dangerous boy! Enough, you're too sharp.
DUCHESS. Good lady, don't be angry with the child.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Little pitchers have big ears.
Enter a Messenger.
ARCHBISHOP. Here comes a messenger. What news?
MESSENGER. News, my lord, that grieves me to report.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. How is the Prince?
MESSENGER. Well, madam, and in good health.
DUCHESS. What is your news?
MESSENGER. Lord Rivers and Lord Grey have been sent to Pomfret as prisoners, and with them Sir Thomas Vaughan.
DUCHESS. Who has imprisoned them?
MESSENGER. The mighty Dukes, Gloucester and Buckingham.
ARCHBISHOP. For what offense?
MESSENGER. I have told you everything I can. Why or for what reason the nobles were arrested, I don't know at all, my gracious lord.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh no! I see the ruin of my house. The tiger has now seized the gentle doe. Insolent tyranny begins to thrust itself upon the innocent throne that has no power to inspire fear. Welcome, destruction, blood and massacre. I see the end of everything, as if on a map.

DUCHESS. Cursed, restless days of quarreling, how many of you have my eyes seen! My husband lost his life to win the crown. My sons were tossed back and forth, and I had to rejoice and weep over their gains and losses. And once they were seated on the throne and the domestic troubles had completely blown over, the conquerors themselves made war on each other: brother against brother, blood against blood, self against self. Oh, this perverse and frantic madness, end your damned spite, or let me die and look on earth no more.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Come, come, my boy. We will go to sanctuary. Madam, farewell.
DUCHESS. Wait, I will go with you.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. You have no reason to.
ARCHBISHOP.
[_To the Queen._] My gracious lady, go,

And take your treasure and your goods there. As for me, I'll hand over to you the seal that I keep. And may things go for me exactly as I care for you and all your family. Go, I'll escort you to the sanctuary.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — London. A street
paragraphs: The trumpets sound. Enter young Prince Edward, Richard, Buckingham, Cardinal Bourchier, Catesby and others.
BUCKINGHAM. Welcome, sweet Prince, to London, to your chamber.
RICHARD. Welcome, dear nephew, sovereign of my thoughts. The tiring journey has made you gloomy.
PRINCE. No, uncle. It was the troubles on the way that made it tedious, wearisome and heavy. I wish I had more uncles here to welcome me.

RICHARD. Sweet Prince, your years are innocent and have not yet dived into the world's deceit. You can no more judge a man than by his outward show, which, God knows, seldom or never matches the heart. Those uncles you miss were dangerous. Your Grace listened to their sugared words but never looked at the poison in their hearts. God keep you from them, and from such false friends!
PRINCE. God keep me from false friends, but they were not false.
RICHARD. My lord, the Mayor of London is coming to greet you.
Enter Lord Mayor with Attendants.
MAYOR. God bless your Grace with health and happy days!

PRINCE. I thank you, good my lord, and I thank you all. I thought my mother and my brother York would have met us on the road long before now. Shame on Hastings, what a slug he is, that he doesn't come to tell us whether they're coming or not!
Enter Lord Hastings.
BUCKINGHAM. And just in time, here comes the sweating lord.
PRINCE. Welcome, my lord. What, is our mother coming?

HASTINGS. For what reason, God knows, not I. The Queen your mother and your brother York have taken sanctuary. The young prince would gladly have come with me to meet your Grace, but his mother kept him back by force.

BUCKINGHAM. Shame! What a devious and peevish thing for her to do! Lord Cardinal, will your Grace persuade the Queen to send the Duke of York to his princely brother at once? If she refuses, Lord Hastings, go with him and pull him by force out of her jealous arms.

CARDINAL. My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak speaking can win the Duke of York from his mother, expect him here soon. But if she stays stubborn against gentle pleading, God in heaven forbid that we should violate the holy privilege of blessed sanctuary! Not for all this land would I be guilty of so deep a sin.

BUCKINGHAM. You are too senselessly stubborn, my lord, too ceremonious and bound by tradition. Weigh it against the crudeness of this age, and you won't be breaking sanctuary by seizing him. Its benefit is always granted to those whose actions have earned the place, and to those who have the wit to claim it. This prince has neither claimed it nor earned it, and so, in my opinion, he cannot have it. So if you take him from a place where he isn't, you break no privilege or charter there. I have often heard of sanctuary men, but sanctuary children, never until now.
CARDINAL. My lord, you shall overrule my mind for once. Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
HASTINGS. I go, my lord.
PRINCE. Good lords, make all the speed you can.
[_Exeunt Cardinal and Hastings._]
Tell me, uncle Gloucester, when our brother comes, where will we stay until our coronation?

RICHARD. Wherever seems best to your royal self. If I may advise you, Your Highness could rest for a day or two at the Tower. Then you can go wherever you please and think most fitting for your health and recreation.
PRINCE. Of all places, I don't like the Tower. Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?
BUCKINGHAM. He did, my gracious lord, begin it, and later ages have rebuilt it.
PRINCE. Is it on record, or only reported from age to age, that he built it?
BUCKINGHAM. On record, my gracious lord.

PRINCE. But say, my lord, that it were not written down. I think the truth should live on from age to age, as if it were passed on to all future generations, even to the final day that ends everything.
RICHARD.
[_Aside_.] So wise so young, they say, never live long.
PRINCE. What did you say, uncle?
RICHARD. I say that fame lives long even without written letters.
[_Aside_.] Thus, like the stock Vice, Iniquity in the old plays,
I draw two meanings from one word.

PRINCE. That Julius Caesar was a famous man. His courage fed his intelligence, and his intelligence wrote it down to keep his courage alive. Death makes no conquest of this conqueror, for now he lives in fame, though not in life. I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham.
BUCKINGHAM. What, my gracious lord?
PRINCE. If I live until I'm a man, I'll win back our ancient right in France, or die a soldier, as I lived a king.
RICHARD.
[_Aside_.] Short summers usually have an early spring.
Enter young Duke of York, Hastings and the Cardinal.
BUCKINGHAM. And just in time, here comes the Duke of York.
PRINCE. Richard of York, how is our loving brother?
YORK. Well, my dread lord, for so I must call you now.
PRINCE. Yes, brother, to our grief, as it is yours. He died too soon who could have kept that title, which has lost much majesty by his death.
RICHARD. How is our nephew, the noble lord of York?
YORK. I thank you, gentle uncle. Oh, my lord, you said that idle weeds grow fast. The Prince my brother has outgrown me by far.
RICHARD. He has, my lord.
YORK. And so is he idle?
RICHARD. Oh, my fair nephew, I must not say so.
YORK. Then he owes you more than I do.
RICHARD. He may command me as my sovereign, but you have power over me as a kinsman.
YORK. Please, uncle, give me this dagger.
RICHARD. My dagger, little nephew? With all my heart.
PRINCE. A beggar, brother?
YORK. Of my kind uncle, who I know will give it, since it's only a toy and no grief to give away.
RICHARD. I'll give my nephew a greater gift than that.
YORK. A greater gift? Oh, that's the sword that goes with it.
RICHARD. Yes, gentle nephew, if it were light enough.
YORK. Oh, then I see you will part only with light gifts. In weightier things you'll tell a beggar no.
RICHARD. It is too heavy for your Grace to wear.
YORK. I'd treat it lightly, even if it were heavier.
RICHARD. What, would you have my weapon, little lord?
YORK. I would, so that I might thank you as you call me.
RICHARD. How?
YORK. Little.
PRINCE. My lord of York will always be contrary in talk. Uncle, your Grace knows how to put up with him.
YORK. You mean carry me, not put up with me. Uncle, my brother mocks both you and me. Because I am little, like an ape, he thinks you should carry me on your shoulders.
BUCKINGHAM. With what a sharp wit he argues! To soften the scorn he gives his uncle, he neatly and cleverly mocks himself. To be so cunning and so young is wonderful.
RICHARD. My lord, will you please walk along? My good cousin Buckingham and I will go to your mother and ask her to meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
YORK. What, are you going to the Tower, my lord?
PRINCE. My Lord Protector insists on it.
YORK. I shall not sleep in peace at the Tower.
RICHARD. Why, what should you fear?
YORK. Why, my uncle Clarence's angry ghost. My grandmother told me he was murdered there.
PRINCE. I fear no dead uncles.
RICHARD. Nor any living ones, I hope.
PRINCE. If they live, I hope I need not fear them. But come, my lord. With a heavy heart, thinking of them, I go to the Tower.
[_A Sennet. Exeunt Prince Edward, York, Hastings, Dorset and all but Richard, Buckingham and Catesby._]
BUCKINGHAM. Do you think, my lord, that this little chattering York was not stirred up by his cunning mother to taunt and scorn you so insultingly?
RICHARD. No doubt, no doubt. Oh, he's a dangerous boy: bold, quick, clever, forward, capable. He is all his mother's, from top to toe.

BUCKINGHAM. Well, let them rest. Come here, Catesby. You are sworn as deeply to carry out what we intend as to keep secret what we tell you. You know our reasons, which we laid out on the road. What do you think? Is it an easy matter to bring William, Lord Hastings, around to our mind, so that this noble Duke can be installed on the royal throne of this famous island?
CATESBY. For his father's sake he loves the Prince so much that he will not be won over to anything against him.
BUCKINGHAM. What do you think of Stanley, then? Won't he?
CATESBY. He will do just as Hastings does, in everything.

BUCKINGHAM. Well then, no more than this. Go, gentle Catesby, and, as if from far off, sound out Lord Hastings on how he feels about our purpose. Summon him tomorrow to the Tower to sit in on the coronation. If you find him willing to follow us, encourage him and tell him all our reasons. If he is leaden, icy, cold and unwilling, be so yourself, break off the talk, and let us know what he's inclined to do. For tomorrow we hold separate councils, in which you yourself will be highly employed.
