RICHARD. Give my greetings to Lord William. Tell him, Catesby, that his old band of dangerous enemies will be let blood at Pomfret Castle tomorrow. And tell my lord, for joy at this good news, to give Mistress Shore one gentle kiss more.
BUCKINGHAM. Good Catesby, go and carry out this business soundly.
CATESBY. My good lords both, with all the care I can.
RICHARD. Shall we hear from you, Catesby, before we sleep?
CATESBY. You shall, my lord.
RICHARD. You will find us both at Crosby Place.
[_Exit Catesby._]
BUCKINGHAM. Now, my lord, what shall we do if we see that Lord Hastings will not give in to our plots?
RICHARD. Chop off his head, man. We'll do something. And remember, when I am king, claim from me the earldom of Hereford and all the movable goods the King my brother owned.
BUCKINGHAM. I'll claim that promise from your Grace.
RICHARD. And expect to have it granted with all kindness. Come, let's have supper early, so that afterward we can work out our plots in some order.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Before Lord Hastings’ house
paragraphs: Enter a Messenger to the door of Hastings.
MESSENGER. My lord, my lord!
[_Knocking._]
HASTINGS.
[_Within_.] Who's knocking?
MESSENGER. A man from Lord Stanley.
HASTINGS.
[_Within_.] What time is it?
MESSENGER. Just striking four.
Enter Hastings.
HASTINGS. Can't my Lord Stanley sleep through these long nights?
MESSENGER. So it seems from what I have to say. First, he sends his greetings to your noble self.
HASTINGS. What then?

MESSENGER. Then he informs your lordship that tonight he dreamed the boar had torn off his helmet. Besides, he says there are two councils being held, and something may be decided at one that could make you and him regret it at the other. So he sends to learn your lordship's wishes: whether you will take horse with him right away and ride with him in all haste toward the north, to avoid the danger his soul foresees.

HASTINGS. Go, fellow, go. Go back to your lord. Tell him not to fear the separate council. His honor and I are at one of them, and at the other is my good friend Catesby. Nothing can go on there that touches us without my hearing of it. Tell him his fears are shallow and have nothing to back them. As for his dreams, I wonder he's so foolish as to trust the mockery of restless sleep. To run from the boar before the boar chases us would only provoke the boar to follow us, and to hunt where he never meant to chase. Go, tell your master to get up and come to me, and we will go together to the Tower, where he will see the boar treat us kindly.
MESSENGER. I'll go, my lord, and tell him what you say.
[_Exit._]
Enter Catesby.
CATESBY. Many good mornings to my noble lord.
HASTINGS. Good morning, Catesby. You're up early. What news, what news in this shaky state of ours?
CATESBY. It is a reeling world indeed, my lord, and I believe it will never stand upright until Richard wears the garland of the realm.
HASTINGS. What, wear the garland? Do you mean the crown?
CATESBY. Yes, my good lord.
HASTINGS. I'd have this head of mine cut from my shoulders before I'd see the crown so foully misplaced. But can you guess that he aims at it?

CATESBY. Yes, on my life, and he hopes to find you eager on his side for the sake of the gain. And so he sends you this good news: this very day your enemies, the Queen's kindred, must die at Pomfret.

HASTINGS. Indeed, I'm no mourner for that news, because they have always been my enemies. But I will not give my vote to Richard's side to bar my master's heirs from their rightful inheritance. God knows I won't do it, even if it costs my life.
CATESBY. God keep your lordship in that gracious mind.

HASTINGS. But I shall laugh at this a year from now: that I live to look upon the tragedy of those who made my master hate me. Well, Catesby, before another fortnight makes me older, I'll send packing some who don't yet think of it.
CATESBY. It's a vile thing to die, my gracious lord, when men are unprepared and don't expect it.

HASTINGS. Oh, monstrous, monstrous! And that is just how it turns out for Rivers, Vaughan and Grey. And so it will for some other men who think themselves as safe as you and I, who, as you know, are dear to princely Richard and to Buckingham.
CATESBY. Both Dukes think highly of you —
[_Aside_.] Yes, they value your head so much they already count it as good as set on London Bridge.
HASTINGS. I know they do, and I have well deserved it.
Enter Stanley Earl of Derby.
Come on, come on. Where is your boar-spear, man? Do you fear the boar, and yet go so unarmed?
STANLEY. My lord, good morning. Good morning, Catesby. You may joke on, but, by the Holy Cross, I don't like these separate councils.

HASTINGS. My lord, I value my life as dearly as you value yours, and never in my days, I swear, has it been as precious to me as it is now. Do you think I would be as triumphant as I am if I didn't know our position was secure?

STANLEY. The lords at Pomfret, when they rode out of London, were cheerful and thought their positions safe, and they truly had no cause for distrust. And yet you see how quickly the day clouded over. I distrust this sudden stab of malice. I pray God, I say, that I prove a needless coward. What, shall we go toward the Tower? The day is wearing on.
HASTINGS. Come, come. I'm with you. Do you know what, my lord? Today the lords you spoke of are beheaded.
STANLEY. For their loyalty, they might better keep their heads than some who accused them keep their hats. But come, my lord, let's go.
Enter a Pursuivant.
HASTINGS. Go on ahead. I'll talk with this good fellow.
[_Exeunt Stanley and Catesby._]
Well, sirrah? How goes the world with you?
PURSUIVANT. All the better for your lordship's asking.

HASTINGS. I tell you, man, it's better with me now than when you last met me on this very spot. Then I was going to the Tower as a prisoner, because of the Queen's allies. But now, I tell you, and keep it to yourself, those enemies are being put to death today, and I'm in a better position than I've ever been.
PURSUIVANT. God keep it so, to your honor's content!
HASTINGS. Thank you, fellow. Here, drink that for me.
[_Throws him his purse._]
PURSUIVANT. I thank your honor.
[_Exit._]
Enter a Priest.
PRIEST. Well met, my lord. I'm glad to see your honor.
HASTINGS. I thank you with all my heart, good Sir John. I am in your debt for your last service. Come next Sunday, and I will pay you.
Enter Buckingham.
PRIEST. I'll wait on your lordship.
[_Exit Priest._]
BUCKINGHAM. What, talking with a priest, Lord Chamberlain? Your friends at Pomfret are the ones who need a priest. Your honor has no confessing to do.
HASTINGS. Honestly, when I met this holy man, the men you speak of came into my mind. What, are you going toward the Tower?
BUCKINGHAM. I am, my lord, but I can't stay there long. I shall be back before your lordship leaves.
HASTINGS. No, that's likely, for I'm staying there for dinner.
BUCKINGHAM.
[_Aside_.] And supper too, although you don't know it.
Come, will you go?
HASTINGS. I'll wait on your lordship.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Pomfret. Before the Castle
paragraphs: Enter Sir Richard Ratcliffe, with Halberds, carrying the nobles Rivers, Grey and Vaughan to death at Pomfret.
RIVERS. Sir Richard Ratcliffe, let me tell you this: today you will watch a subject die for truth, for duty and for loyalty.
GREY. God protect the Prince from all of you! You are a pack of damned bloodsuckers.
VAUGHAN You who live will cry woe for this hereafter.
RATCLIFFE Hurry up. The limit of your lives has run out.

RIVERS. Oh Pomfret, Pomfret! Oh you bloody prison, fatal and ominous to noble peers! Within the guilty enclosure of your walls Richard the Second was hacked to death. And, to add more slander to your dismal seat, we give you our guiltless blood to drink.
GREY. Now Margaret's curse has fallen on our heads, when she cried out against Hastings, you and me, for standing by when Richard stabbed her son.

RIVERS. Then she cursed Richard, then she cursed Buckingham, then she cursed Hastings. Oh, God, remember to hear her prayer for them, as now for us! And for my sister and her princely sons, be satisfied, dear God, with our honest blood, which, as you know, is being spilled unjustly.
RATCLIFFE. Make haste. The hour of your death has come.
RIVERS. Come, Grey, come, Vaughan, let us embrace here. Farewell, until we meet again in heaven.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — London. A Room in the Tower
paragraphs: Enter Buckingham, Stanley Earl of Derby, Hastings, the Bishop of Ely, Norfolk, Ratcliffe, Lovell with others, at a table.
HASTINGS. Now, noble peers, we have met to settle the coronation. In God's name, speak. When is the royal day?
BUCKINGHAM. Is everything ready for that royal time?
STANLEY. It is, and only needs a date to be named.
ELY. Tomorrow, then, I judge a happy day.
BUCKINGHAM. Who knows the Lord Protector's mind on this? Who is closest to the noble Duke?
ELY. Your Grace, we think, would soonest know his mind.
BUCKINGHAM. We know each other's faces, but as for our hearts, he knows no more of mine than I know of yours, or I of his, my lord, than you of mine. Lord Hastings, you and he are close friends.

HASTINGS. I thank his Grace, I know he loves me well. But as for his intention about the coronation, I have not sounded him out, and he has not told me his gracious wishes on it in any way. But you, my honorable lords, may name the time, and I'll give my vote on the Duke's behalf, which I expect he'll take kindly.
Enter Richard.
ELY. In good time, here comes the Duke himself.
RICHARD. My noble lords and cousins all, good morning. I've been a long sleeper. But I trust my absence has not neglected any great plan that my presence could have settled.
BUCKINGHAM. If you hadn't come right on your cue, my lord, William, Lord Hastings, would have spoken your part. I mean your vote for crowning the King.

RICHARD. No man could be bolder than my Lord Hastings. His lordship knows me well and loves me well. My lord of Ely, when I was last in Holborn I saw good strawberries in your garden there. I beg you, send for some of them.
ELY. Indeed I will, my lord, with all my heart.
[_Exit._]
RICHARD. Cousin of Buckingham, a word with you.
[_They move aside._]

Catesby has sounded out Hastings about our business. He finds the touchy gentleman so hot that he would lose his head before he'd agree that his master's child, as he respectfully calls him, should lose the royalty of England's throne.
BUCKINGHAM. Step aside for a while. I'll go with you.
[_Exeunt Richard and Buckingham._]
STANLEY. We haven't yet fixed this day of triumph. Tomorrow, in my judgment, is too sudden. I myself am not as well prepared as I would be if the day were put off.
Enter Bishop of Ely.
ELY. Where is my lord the Duke of Gloucester? I have sent for those strawberries.

HASTINGS. His Grace looks cheerful and smooth this morning. Some thought or other pleases him well when he says good morning with such spirit. I think there's no man in Christendom who can hide his love or hate less than he can. You can tell his heart straight from his face.
STANLEY. What do you see of his heart in his face, from any sign he showed today?
HASTINGS. Why, that he's offended with no man here. If he were, he would have shown it in his looks.
Enter Richard and Buckingham.
RICHARD. I ask you all, tell me what they deserve who plot my death with devilish schemes of damned witchcraft, and who have worked on my body with their hellish charms?
HASTINGS. The tender love I bear your Grace, my lord, makes me the most ready, in this princely company, to pass sentence on the offenders, whoever they are. I say, my lord, they have deserved death.

RICHARD. Then let your own eyes witness their evil. Look how I am bewitched! See, my arm is like a blasted sapling, withered up! And this is Edward's wife, that monstrous witch, in league with that harlot, that strumpet Shore, who by their witchcraft have marked me like this.
HASTINGS. If they have done this deed, my noble lord —

RICHARD. If? You protector of this damned strumpet, do you talk to me of "ifs"? You are a traitor. Off with his head! Now by Saint Paul I swear I will not dine until I see it done. Lovell and Ratcliffe, make sure it's done. The rest of you who love me, rise and follow me.
[_Exeunt all but Lovell and Ratcliffe with the Lord Hastings._]

HASTINGS. Woe, woe for England! Not a bit for me. I, too foolish, could have prevented this. Stanley dreamed the boar tore off his helmet, and I scorned it and refused to run. Three times today my horse stumbled, and shied when it looked at the Tower, as if it hated to carry me to the slaughterhouse. Oh, now I need the priest who spoke to me. Now I repent that I told the pursuivant, too triumphantly, how my enemies were bloodily butchered at Pomfret today, while I myself was safe in grace and favor. Oh Margaret, Margaret, now your heavy curse has fallen on poor Hastings's wretched head.
RATCLIFFE. Come, come, hurry. The Duke wants to be at dinner. Make your confession short. He longs to see your head.

HASTINGS. Oh, the fleeting favor of mortal men, which we hunt more eagerly than the favor of God! Whoever builds his hope on the air of your good looks lives like a drunken sailor on a mast, ready at every nod to tumble down into the deadly depths of the sea.
LOVELL. Come, come, hurry. It's no use to cry out.

HASTINGS. Oh bloody Richard! Miserable England, I prophesy the most fearful time for you that any wretched age has ever seen. Come, lead me to the block. Bring him my head. They smile at me who will shortly be dead.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — London. The Tower Walls
paragraphs: Enter Richard and Buckingham in rotten armour, marvellous ill-favoured.
RICHARD. Come, cousin, can you shake with fear and change your color, choke off your breath in the middle of a word, then start again and stop again, as if you were out of your mind with terror?

BUCKINGHAM. Ha, I can imitate the deep tragic actor. I can speak, look back, peer on every side, and tremble and start at the wagging of a straw, showing deep suspicion. Ghastly looks are at my service, like forced smiles, and both are ready to do their jobs at any time to grace my schemes. But what, is Catesby gone?
RICHARD. He is. And see, he brings the Mayor along.
Enter the Lord Mayor and Catesby.
BUCKINGHAM. Lord Mayor —
RICHARD. Watch the drawbridge there!
BUCKINGHAM. Listen, a drum.
RICHARD. Catesby, look over the walls.
BUCKINGHAM. Lord Mayor, the reason we have sent —
RICHARD. Look back! Defend yourself, here are enemies.
BUCKINGHAM. God and our innocence defend and guard us!
Enter Lovell and Ratcliffe with Hastings' head.
RICHARD. Be calm, they are friends, Ratcliffe and Lovell.
LOVELL. Here is the head of that ignoble traitor, the dangerous and unsuspected Hastings.

RICHARD. I loved the man so dearly that I must weep. I took him for the plainest, most harmless creature that ever breathed on earth as a Christian. I made him my book, in which my soul recorded the history of all her secret thoughts. He painted his vice so smoothly with a show of virtue that, leaving aside his obvious open guilt, I mean his dealings with Shore's wife, he lived free of any suspicion of treason.

BUCKINGHAM. Well, well, he was the most secretly sheltered traitor that ever lived. Would you imagine, or even believe, if it weren't that by great good fortune we survive to tell it, that the cunning traitor had planned this very day, in the council house, to murder me and my good lord of Gloucester?
MAYOR. Had he done so?

RICHARD. What, do you think we are Turks or infidels? Or that we would, against the form of law, proceed so rashly to the villain's death, if the extreme danger of the case, the peace of England and the safety of our own persons had not forced us to this execution?
MAYOR. Now, good fortune to you! He deserved his death, and your good Graces have both acted well, to warn false traitors off such attempts.

BUCKINGHAM. I never expected better from him after he once fell in with Mistress Shore. Yet we had not decided that he should die until your lordship came to see his end. The loving haste of these our friends, somewhat against our intentions, has prevented that. We wanted you to have heard the traitor speak and fearfully confess the manner and purpose of his treasons, so that you could report it to the citizens, who might otherwise misjudge us in this and mourn his death.

MAYOR. But, my good lord, your Grace's word will serve as well as if I had seen and heard him speak. And do not doubt, most noble princes both, that I will inform our dutiful citizens of all your just proceedings in this case.
RICHARD. And to that end we wished your lordship here, to avoid the criticism of the carping world.
BUCKINGHAM. But since you came too late for our purpose, still bear witness to what you hear we intended. And so, my good Lord Mayor, we bid you farewell.
[_Exit Lord Mayor._]

RICHARD. Go after him, after him, cousin Buckingham. The Mayor is hurrying to the Guildhall in all haste. There, at the best moment you can find, suggest that Edward's children are bastards. Tell them how Edward put a citizen to death only for saying he would make his son heir to the Crown, meaning in fact his house, which was named "the Crown" from the sign above its door. Moreover, press his hateful lust and beastly appetite for changing partners, which stretched to their servants, daughters and wives, wherever his raging eye or savage heart, unchecked, wanted to make a prey. Indeed, if need be, come this near to my own person: tell them that when my mother was pregnant with that insatiable Edward, my noble father York was then at war in France. By a true count of the time, he found that the child was not begotten by him. That showed plainly in his features, which were nothing like my noble father the Duke. Yet touch on this lightly, as if from far off, because, my lord, you know my mother is alive.
BUCKINGHAM. Do not doubt, my lord, I'll play the orator as if the golden fee I plead for were for myself. And so, my lord, goodbye.
RICHARD. If you succeed, bring them to Baynard's Castle, where you will find me well accompanied by reverend fathers and learned bishops.
BUCKINGHAM. I go. Expect the news from the Guildhall around three or four o'clock.
[_Exit._]
RICHARD. Go, Lovell, with all speed to Doctor Shaa.
[_To Ratcliffe_.] You go to Friar Penker. Tell them both
to meet me within the hour at Baynard's Castle.
[_Exeunt Ratcliffe and Lovell._]
Now I will go and make some private arrangements to get Clarence's brats out of sight, and to give orders that no one at all has access to the Princes at any time.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 6 — London. A street
paragraphs: Enter a Scrivener.

SCRIVENER. Here is the indictment of the good Lord Hastings, neatly copied out in a formal hand, so that it can be read aloud in St. Paul's today. And note how well the sequence hangs together. I have spent eleven hours writing it out, for Catesby sent it to me only last night. The draft took just as long to prepare, and yet within these five hours Hastings was alive, untainted, unquestioned, free and at liberty. A fine world we live in! Who is so dull that he can't see this obvious trick? Yet who is so bold as to say he sees it? The world is bad, and all will come to nothing when such foul dealing must be seen only in thought.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 7 — London. Court of Baynard’s Castle
paragraphs: Enter Richard and Buckingham at several doors.
RICHARD. Well, well? What do the citizens say?
BUCKINGHAM. By the holy mother of our Lord, the citizens are dumb. They won't say a word.
RICHARD. Did you bring up the bastardy of Edward's children?

BUCKINGHAM. I did. I told them about Edward's contract with Lady Lucy and his contract by proxy in France. I told them about his insatiable greed, his forcing himself on the wives of the city, and his tyranny over trifles. I told them about his own bastardy: he was conceived while your father was in France, and he looks nothing like the Duke. Then I turned to you. I said you are the very image of your father, in your looks and in your noble mind. I laid out all your victories in Scotland, your discipline in war, your wisdom in peace, your generosity, your virtue and your gentle humility. In fact, I left out nothing that suited our purpose, or touched on it only lightly. And when my speech was nearly over, I told everyone who loved their country's good to cry "God save Richard, England's royal King!"
RICHARD. And did they?

BUCKINGHAM. No, so help me God, they said not a word. They stared at each other like dumb statues or breathing stones, and they went deadly pale. When I saw that, I scolded them. I asked the Mayor what this stubborn silence meant. He answered that the people were not used to being spoken to by anyone but the Recorder. So he was pressed to repeat my speech: "Thus says the Duke, thus the Duke has argued." But he added nothing of his own. When he finished, some of my own men at the far end of the hall threw up their caps, and about ten voices cried, "God save King Richard!" I took advantage of those few. "Thank you, kind citizens and friends," I said. "This general applause and cheerful shout shows your wisdom and your love for Richard." And right there I broke off and came away.
RICHARD. What, tongueless blockheads! Wouldn't they speak? Won't the Mayor and his colleagues come, then?

BUCKINGHAM. The Mayor is close by. Pretend to be afraid. Don't let anyone speak with you unless they plead hard. And make sure you have a prayer book in your hand and stand between two churchmen, my good lord. On that ground I'll improvise a holy tune. And don't be easily won over. Play the maiden's part: keep saying no, and take it.
RICHARD. I'm going. If you plead for them as well as I can say no to you for myself, there's no doubt we'll bring this to a happy end.
BUCKINGHAM. Go, go, up to the roof. The Lord Mayor is knocking.
[_Exit Richard._]
Enter the Lord Mayor and Citizens.
Welcome, my lord. I'm kicking my heels here. I think the Duke won't see anyone.
Enter Catesby.
Now, Catesby, what does your lord say to my request?

CATESBY. He asks your Grace, my noble lord, to visit him tomorrow or the next day. He is inside with two most reverend fathers, wholly given to meditation. No worldly business could draw him away from his holy exercise.

BUCKINGHAM. Go back, good Catesby, to the gracious Duke. Tell him that I, the Mayor and the aldermen have come to speak with his Grace on weighty matters of great importance, nothing less than the good of us all.
CATESBY. I'll tell him that right away.
[_Exit._]

BUCKINGHAM. Ah ha, my lord, this prince is no Edward! He isn't lolling on a lewd love-bed, but kneeling in meditation. He isn't playing with a pair of courtesans, but meditating with two deep divines. He isn't sleeping to fatten his idle body, but praying to enrich his watchful soul. England would be happy if this virtuous prince would take the sovereignty on himself. But I'm afraid we won't win him over to it.
MAYOR. Indeed, God forbid his Grace should say no to us!
BUCKINGHAM. I fear he will. Here comes Catesby again.
Enter Catesby.
Now, Catesby, what does his Grace say?
CATESBY. He wonders why you have gathered such crowds of citizens to come to him, when his Grace was not warned of it beforehand. He fears, my lord, that you mean him no good.
BUCKINGHAM. I'm sorry that my noble cousin should suspect I mean him no good. By heaven, we come to him in perfect love. So go back once more and tell his Grace.
[_Exit Catesby._]
When holy and devout men are at their prayer beads, it's hard to draw them away. Zealous contemplation is so sweet.
Enter Richard aloft, between two Bishops. Catesby reenters.
MAYOR. Look, there his Grace stands between two clergymen!

BUCKINGHAM. Two pillars of virtue for a Christian prince, to keep him from falling into vanity. And see, a prayer book in his hand, the true ornaments of a holy man. Famous Plantagenet, most gracious Prince, listen kindly to our requests, and forgive us for interrupting your devotion and your truly Christian zeal.

RICHARD. My lord, there is no need for such an apology. I beg your Grace to forgive me. I was busy in the service of my God, and so I put off receiving my friends. But leaving that aside, what does your Grace wish?
BUCKINGHAM. Just what I hope pleases God above, and all the good men of this ungoverned island.
RICHARD. I suspect I have done something that looks disgraceful in the city's eyes, and that you have come to rebuke me for my ignorance.
BUCKINGHAM. You have, my lord. I wish it would please your Grace, at our request, to mend your fault.
RICHARD. Otherwise, why do I breathe in a Christian land?

BUCKINGHAM. Then know that your fault is this: you give up the supreme seat, the majestic throne, the sceptered office of your ancestors, your rank, your birthright and the lineal glory of your royal house, and you give them to the corruption of a tainted stock. Meanwhile, in the mildness of your sleepy thoughts, which we have come here to wake for our country's good, the noble island lacks her proper limbs. Her face is disfigured with scars of shame. Her royal stock is grafted with ignoble plants. She is almost thrust into the swallowing gulf of dark forgetfulness and deep oblivion. To cure this, we sincerely beg your gracious self to take on the charge and kingly government of this your land. We don't ask you to be Protector, steward, substitute or humble agent working for another's gain. We ask you to be king by right, passed down from blood to blood: your birthright, your empire, your own. For this, together with the citizens, your most respectful and loving friends, and driven by their strong urging, I come in this just cause to move your Grace.

RICHARD. I can't tell whether it suits my rank, or your station, better to leave in silence or to speak bitterly in rebuke. If I don't answer, you might think that tongue-tied ambition, by not replying, has agreed to bear the golden yoke of sovereignty that you foolishly want to put on me. If I rebuke you for this request, which is so full of your faithful love for me, then I would be insulting my friends. So, to speak, and to avoid the first danger without running into the second, I answer you plainly like this: your love deserves my thanks, but my lack of merit rejects your high request. First, even if every obstacle were cleared away and my path to the crown were smooth, as the ripe due of birth, I am still so poor in spirit, and my defects are so great and so many, that I would rather hide from greatness. I am a boat that cannot survive a mighty sea. I would not want, in my greatness, to be hidden and smothered in the vapor of my glory. But thank God, there is no need of me, though I would badly need help if there were. The royal tree has left us royal fruit, which, ripened by the creeping hours of time, will fill the seat of majesty well and surely make us happy by his reign. What you would lay on me, I lay on him: the right and the fortune of his happy stars, which God forbid I should wrench from him.

BUCKINGHAM. My lord, this shows conscience in your Grace. But the scruples behind it are petty and trivial, once everything is considered. You say that Edward is your brother's son. So do we, but not by Edward's wife. He was first contracted to Lady Lucy, and your mother is alive to witness his vow. Afterward he was betrothed by proxy to Bona, sister of the King of France. He broke off both. Then a poor petitioner, a mother of many sons worn out with cares, a widow whose beauty was fading and who was in distress, in the afternoon of her best days, became the prize and purchase of his lustful eye. That eye seduced the height and pitch of his rank down to a base decline and a loathsome bigamy. By her, in his unlawful bed, he fathered this Edward, whom we politely call the Prince. I could complain more bitterly, but out of respect for some who are still alive, I put a limit on my tongue. So, my good lord, take this offered dignity for yourself. If not to bless us and the land, then at least to draw your noble ancestry out of the corruption of abusing times and back onto a true line of descent.
MAYOR. Do it, my good lord. Your citizens beg you.
BUCKINGHAM. Don't refuse this offered love, mighty lord.
CATESBY. Oh, make them joyful. Grant their lawful request.
RICHARD. Alas, why would you heap these cares on me? I am unfit for state and majesty. I beg you, don't take it badly. I cannot, and I will not, yield to you.

BUCKINGHAM. If you refuse, out of love and zeal, unwilling to depose the child, your brother's son — we know well your tenderness of heart and your gentle, kind, womanly pity, which we have seen in you toward your kin, and equally toward everyone of every rank — still, know this, whether you accept our request or not: your brother's son shall never reign as our king. We will put someone else on the throne, to the disgrace and downfall of your house. With that resolution we leave you here. Come, citizens. Damn it, I'll plead no more.
[_Exeunt Buckingham, the Mayor and citizens._]
CATESBY. Call him back, sweet Prince. Accept their request. If you refuse them, the whole land will regret it.
RICHARD. Will you force me into a world of cares? Call them back. I am not made of stone. I can be touched by your kind pleas, even though it goes against my conscience and my soul.
Enter Buckingham and the rest.

Cousin of Buckingham, and wise, grave men, since you will buckle Fortune on my back to bear her burden whether I like it or not, I must have patience to carry the load. But if black scandal or foul-faced reproach follows what you are imposing on me, your pure compulsion will clear me of all the impure blots and stains of it. God knows, and you can partly see, how far I am from wanting this.
MAYOR. God bless your Grace! We see it, and we will say so.
RICHARD. In saying so, you will only say the truth.
BUCKINGHAM. Then I greet you with this royal title: long live King Richard, England's worthy King!
ALL. Amen.
BUCKINGHAM. Would it please you to be crowned tomorrow?
RICHARD. Whenever you please, since you will have it so.
BUCKINGHAM. Then tomorrow we will attend your Grace. And so, most joyfully, we take our leave.
RICHARD.
[_To the Bishops_.] Come, let us return to our holy work.
Farewell, my cousin. Farewell, kind friends.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — London. Before the Tower
paragraphs: Enter Queen Elizabeth, the Duchess of York and Marquess of Dorset, at one door; Anne Duchess of Gloucester with Clarence's young Daughter at another door.

DUCHESS. Who is this coming? My granddaughter Plantagenet, led by the hand of her kind aunt of Gloucester? I'd bet my life she's on her way to the Tower, out of pure love, to greet the young Prince. Granddaughter, well met.
ANNE. God give both your Graces a happy and joyful day.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. The same to you, good sister. Where are you going?
ANNE. No farther than the Tower. And I guess it's from the same devotion as yours: to greet the gentle Princes there.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Thank you, kind sister. We'll go in together.
Enter Brakenbury.
And just in time, here comes the Lieutenant. Master Lieutenant, if you please, how are the Prince and my young son of York?
BRAKENBURY. Very well, dear madam. With your patience, I cannot allow you to visit them. The King has strictly ordered otherwise.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. The King? Who is that?
BRAKENBURY. I mean the Lord Protector.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. May the Lord protect him from that kingly title! Has he set a barrier between their love and me? I am their mother. Who will keep me from them?
DUCHESS. I am their father's mother. I will see them.
ANNE. I am their aunt by marriage and their mother in love. So take me to see them. I'll take the blame, and I'll take your post from you, at my own risk.
BRAKENBURY. No, madam, no. I cannot leave it like this. I am bound by oath, so forgive me.
[_Exit._]
Enter Stanley.
STANLEY. Let me meet you, ladies, one hour from now, and I'll greet your Grace of York as the mother and revered onlooker of two fair queens.
[_To Anne._] Come, madam, you must go straight to Westminster,
There you will be crowned Richard's royal queen.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, cut my laces apart so my cramped heart has room to beat, or else I'll faint at this deadly news!
ANNE. Spiteful tidings! Oh, unwelcome news!
DORSET. Cheer up, mother. How are you, your Grace?

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh Dorset, don't speak to me. Get away. Death and destruction are snapping at your heels. Your mother's name is ill-omened for children. If you want to outrun death, go, cross the sea, and live with Richmond, out of the reach of hell. Go, hurry, hurry out of this slaughterhouse, or you will add to the number of the dead and make me die the slave of Margaret's curse, neither mother, wife, nor England's acknowledged Queen.

STANLEY. Your advice is full of wise care, madam. Take full advantage of every hour. You'll have letters from me to my son on your behalf, to meet you on the way. Don't be caught out by foolish delay.
DUCHESS. Oh, ill-scattering wind of misery! Oh, my accursed womb, the bed of death! You hatched a cockatrice into the world, whose unavoidable eye is murderous.
STANLEY. Come, madam, come. I was sent in all haste.

ANNE. And I go with all unwillingness. Oh, I wish to God that the circle of golden metal that must go around my brow were red-hot steel to sear me to the brain. Let me be anointed with deadly venom, and die before men can say "God save the Queen."
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Go, go, poor soul. I don't envy your glory. To feed my mood, wish yourself no harm.

ANNE. No? Why not? When the man who is now my husband came to me as I followed Henry's corpse, when the blood was scarcely washed from his hands, the blood that came from my other husband, an angel, and from that dear saint whom I followed weeping — oh, when, I say, I looked at Richard's face, this was my wish: "May you be accursed," I said, "for making me, so young, such an old widow. And when you marry, may sorrow haunt your bed. May your wife, if any woman is so mad, be made more miserable by your life than you have made me by my dear lord's death." See, before I could finish repeating this curse, in so short a time, my woman's heart was crudely taken captive by his honeyed words. It became the target of my own soul's curse, which has kept my eyes from rest ever since. For never once did I enjoy the golden dew of sleep for one hour in his bed. His fearful dreams always woke me. Besides, he hates me because of my father Warwick, and he will no doubt soon be rid of me.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Poor heart, farewell. I pity your complaining.
ANNE. No more than I mourn for yours, with all my soul.
DORSET. Farewell, you woeful welcomer of glory.
ANNE. Farewell, poor soul, who takes your leave of it.
DUCHESS.
[_To Dorset._] Go to Richmond, and may good fortune guide you.
[_To Anne._] Go to Richard, and may good angels attend you.
[_To Queen Elizabeth._] Go to sanctuary, and may good thoughts possess
you. I go to my grave, where peace and rest lie with me. I have seen eighty-odd years of sorrow, and each hour's joy has been wrecked by a week of grief.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Wait, and look back with me at the Tower. Pity, you ancient stones, those tender babes whom spite has walled up inside you. A rough cradle for such pretty little ones, a rude ragged nurse, an old sullen playfellow for tender princes: treat my babies well. So my foolish sorrow says farewell to your stones.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — London. A Room of State in the Palace
paragraphs: The trumpets sound a sennet. Enter Richard in pomp, Buckingham, Catesby, Ratcliffe, Lovell, a Page and others.
KING RICHARD. Everyone stand back. Cousin of Buckingham!
BUCKINGHAM. My gracious sovereign!
KING RICHARD. Give me your hand.
[_Here he ascendeth the throne. Sound trumpets._]
This high, by your advice and your help, King Richard is seated. But will we wear these glories for a single day, or will they last, so that we can enjoy them?
BUCKINGHAM. May they live on, and last forever!
KING RICHARD. Ah, Buckingham, now I play the touchstone, to test whether you are truly current gold. Young Edward lives. Think now what I'm about to say.
BUCKINGHAM. Say on, my loving lord.
KING RICHARD. Why, Buckingham, I'm saying I want to be King.
BUCKINGHAM. Why, so you are, my thrice-renowned lord.
KING RICHARD. Ha! Am I King? It's true, but Edward lives.
BUCKINGHAM. True, noble Prince.

KING RICHARD. Oh, bitter consequence, that Edward should still live, "true noble prince!" Cousin, you were never so dull before. Shall I be plain? I want the bastards dead, and I want it done quickly. What do you say now? Speak quickly, and be brief.
BUCKINGHAM. Your Grace may do as you please.
KING RICHARD. Tut, tut, you are all ice. Your kindness freezes. Tell me, do I have your consent that they shall die?
BUCKINGHAM. Give me a little time to breathe, a pause, dear lord, before I answer you outright on this. I will give you my decision shortly.
[_Exit._]
CATESBY.
[_Aside_.] The King is angry. See, he's biting his lip.
KING RICHARD.
[_Aside_.] I will deal with iron-witted fools
and thoughtless boys. No one who looks into me with careful eyes is any use to me. High-reaching Buckingham is growing cautious. Boy!
PAGE. My lord?
KING RICHARD. Do you know anyone whom corrupting gold would tempt into a secret killing?
PAGE. I know a discontented gentleman whose humble means don't match his haughty spirit. Gold would work as well as twenty speakers, and it will surely tempt him to anything.
KING RICHARD. What is his name?
PAGE. His name, my lord, is Tyrrel.
KING RICHARD. I know the man a little. Go, call him here, boy.
[_Exit Page._]
[_Aside_.] The deep-brooding, clever Buckingham
will no longer be a neighbor to my counsels. Has he kept up with me so long without tiring, and does he stop for breath now? Well, so be it.
Enter Stanley.
Well, Lord Stanley, what's the news?
STANLEY. Know, my loving lord, that the Marquess Dorset, as I hear, has fled to Richmond, in the region where he stays.

KING RICHARD. Come here, Catesby. Spread the rumor abroad that my wife Anne is very seriously sick. I will arrange to keep her shut away. Find me some poor, humble gentleman, whom I will marry straight away to Clarence's daughter. The boy is foolish, and I don't fear him. Look how you daydream! I say again, give it out that Anne, my Queen, is sick and likely to die. Get to it, for it matters greatly to me to stop every hope whose growth could damage me.
[_Exit Catesby._]

I must marry my brother's daughter, or else my kingdom stands on brittle glass. Murder her brothers, and then marry her. An uncertain way to gain! But I am in so deep in blood that sin will drag on sin. Tear-falling pity does not live in this eye.
Enter Tyrrel.
Is your name Tyrrel?
TYRREL. James Tyrrel, and your most obedient subject.
KING RICHARD. Are you indeed?
TYRREL. Put me to the test, my gracious lord.
KING RICHARD. Do you dare resolve to kill a friend of mine?
TYRREL. If you please. But I would rather kill two enemies.
KING RICHARD. Why then, you have it. Two deadly enemies, foes to my rest and disturbers of my sweet sleep, are the ones I want you to deal with. Tyrrel, I mean those bastards in the Tower.
TYRREL. Give me open means to get to them, and I'll soon rid you of the fear of them.
KING RICHARD. You sing sweet music. Listen, come here, Tyrrel. Go, with this token. Rise, and lend me your ear.
[_Whispers_.] That's all there is. Say it is done,
and I will love you, and promote you for it.
TYRREL. I will do it straight away.
[_Exit._]
Enter Buckingham.
BUCKINGHAM. My lord, I have thought over the request you sounded me out on a while ago.
KING RICHARD. Well, let that rest. Dorset has fled to Richmond.
BUCKINGHAM. I hear the news, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Stanley, he is your wife's son. Well, see to it.
BUCKINGHAM. My lord, I claim the gift that is my due by promise, for which your honor and your word are pledged: the earldom of Hereford, and the movable goods that you promised I should have.
KING RICHARD. Stanley, watch your wife. If she sends letters to Richmond, you will answer for it.
BUCKINGHAM. What does your Highness say to my just request?
KING RICHARD. I remember now. Henry the Sixth prophesied that Richmond would be King, when Richmond was a little peevish boy. A king, perhaps —
BUCKINGHAM. My lord —
KING RICHARD. How did it happen that the prophet could not then have told me, since I was standing by, that I would kill him?
BUCKINGHAM. My lord, your promise of the earldom —

KING RICHARD. Richmond! When I was last at Exeter, the Mayor courteously showed me the castle and called it Rougemount. I started at that name, because an Irish bard once told me I would not live long after I saw Richmond.
BUCKINGHAM. My lord —
KING RICHARD. Yes, what time is it?
BUCKINGHAM. I am bold enough to remind your Grace of what you promised me.
KING RICHARD. Well, but what time is it?
BUCKINGHAM. On the stroke of ten.
KING RICHARD. Well, let it strike.
BUCKINGHAM. Why let it strike?
KING RICHARD. Because, like a clock figure, you keep striking the hour between your begging and my thinking. I am not in a giving mood today.
BUCKINGHAM. Then tell me plainly whether you will or not.
KING RICHARD. You trouble me. I am not in the mood.
[_Exit followed by all save Buckingham._]

BUCKINGHAM. Is it like this? Does he repay my deep service with such contempt? Did I make him King for this? Oh, let me think of Hastings, and be gone to Brecknock while my frightened head is still on!
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — London. Another Room in the Palace
paragraphs: Enter Tyrrel.

TYRREL. The tyrannous, bloody act is done, the most monstrous deed of pitiful slaughter that this land has ever been guilty of. Dighton and Forrest, whom I hired to do this piece of ruthless butchery, were hardened villains and bloody dogs. Yet they melted with tenderness and mild compassion, and wept like two children as they told the sad story of the deaths. "Oh, this is how," said Dighton, "the gentle babes lay." "Like this, like this," said Forrest, "wrapped around each other in their innocent alabaster arms. Their lips were four red roses on one stalk, and in their summer beauty they kissed each other. A prayer book lay on their pillow, which once," said Forrest, "almost changed my mind. But, oh, the devil —" There the villain stopped. Then Dighton went on: "We smothered the most perfect, sweet work of nature that she has ever made since the first creation." After that, both left, so full of conscience and remorse that they could not speak. So I left them both and came to bring this news to the bloody King.
Enter King Richard.
And here he comes. Good health, my sovereign lord.
KING RICHARD. Kind Tyrrel, am I made happy by your news?
TYRREL. If doing what you ordered makes you happy, then be happy, for it is done.
KING RICHARD. But did you see them dead?
TYRREL. I did, my lord.
KING RICHARD. And buried, gentle Tyrrel?
TYRREL. The chaplain of the Tower has buried them, but where, to tell the truth, I do not know.
KING RICHARD. Come to me soon, Tyrrel, after supper, and tell me how they died. Meanwhile, just think about how I can do you good and grant you what you desire. Farewell until then.
TYRREL. I humbly take my leave.
[_Exit._]

KING RICHARD. I have shut up Clarence's son tight. I have married his daughter off to a nobody. Edward's sons sleep in Abraham's bosom, and my wife Anne has said good night to the world. Now, because I know that the Breton Richmond aims at young Elizabeth, my brother's daughter, and hopes by that marriage-knot to look proudly at the crown, I go to her, a cheerful, thriving suitor.
Enter Ratcliffe.
RATCLIFFE. My lord!
KING RICHARD. Is it good or bad news, that you come in so bluntly?
RATCLIFFE. Bad news, my lord. Morton has fled to Richmond, and Buckingham, backed by the hardy Welshmen, is in the field, and his force keeps growing.

KING RICHARD. Ely with Richmond troubles me more closely than Buckingham and his hastily raised army. Come, I have learned that fearful second-guessing is the leaden servant of dull delay. Delay leads to helpless, snail-paced beggary. So let fiery speed be my wing, Jove's Mercury, and herald for a king! Go, muster men. My counsel is my shield. We must be quick when traitors dare to take the field.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — London. Before the Palace
paragraphs: Enter old Queen Margaret.

QUEEN MARGARET. So now prosperity begins to ripen and drop into the rotten mouth of death. I have lurked slyly here in these bounds to watch my enemies decline. I am witness to a dreadful opening act, and I will go to France, hoping the outcome will be as bitter, black and tragic. Hide yourself, wretched Margaret. Who is coming here?
[_Retires._]
Enter Duchess of York and Queen Elizabeth.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, my poor Princes! Ah, my tender babes, my unopened flowers, my sweet new blossoms! If your gentle souls are still flying in the air and are not fixed in everlasting judgment, hover around me with your airy wings and hear your mother's lament.
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside_.] Hover around her, and tell her that justice for justice
has darkened your infant morning into aged night.
DUCHESS. So many miseries have cracked my voice that my woe-weary tongue is still and silent. Edward Plantagenet, why are you dead?
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside_.] Plantagenet pays back Plantagenet.
Edward pays a dying debt for Edward.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Will you, oh God, fly away from such gentle lambs and throw them into the belly of the wolf? When did You sleep, if not when such a deed was done?
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Aside_.] When holy Harry died, and my sweet son.

DUCHESS. Dead life, blind sight, poor mortal living ghost, scene of woe, shame of the world, grave's due taken over by a living body, brief summary and record of tedious days, rest your unrest on England's lawful earth,
[_Sitting_.] which is unlawfully made drunk with innocent blood.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Ah, I wish you would give a grave as readily as you give a melancholy seat. Then I would hide my bones in it, not rest them here.
[_Sitting_.] Ah, who has any cause to mourn but us?
QUEEN MARGARET.
[_Coming forward._]
If the oldest sorrow deserves the most respect, give mine the privilege of the lord of the manor, and let my griefs have the upper hand. If sorrow can bear company,
[_Sitting down with them._]

count over your woes again by looking at mine. I had an Edward, until a Richard killed him. I had a husband, until a Richard killed him. You had an Edward, until a Richard killed him. You had a Richard, until a Richard killed him.
DUCHESS. I had a Richard too, and you killed him. I had a Rutland too, and you helped kill him.

QUEEN MARGARET. You had a Clarence too, and Richard killed him. Out of the kennel of your womb crept a hellhound that hunts us all to death. That dog, which had his teeth before his eyes were open, to worry lambs and lap their gentle blood. That outstanding great tyrant of the earth, who reigns in the sore eyes of weeping souls. That foul defacer of God's handiwork, whom your womb let loose to chase us to our graves. Oh upright, just and rightly ruling God, how I thank you that this carnal cur preys on the offspring of his own mother's body, and makes her a fellow mourner with the groans of others!
DUCHESS. Oh, Harry's wife, don't triumph over my woes! God is my witness, I have wept for yours.

QUEEN MARGARET. Bear with me. I am hungry for revenge, and now I stuff myself by watching it. Your Edward is dead, who killed my Edward. The other Edward is dead, to pay for my Edward. Young York is only the extra thrown in, because neither of those two matched the high perfection of my loss. Your Clarence is dead, who stabbed my Edward. And the onlookers of this frantic play, the adulterous Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan, Grey, have been smothered before their time in their dusky graves. Richard still lives, hell's black spy, kept only as their agent to buy souls and send them there. But soon, very soon, his pitiful and unpitied end follows. Earth gapes, hell burns, fiends roar, saints pray, that he be carried off from here suddenly. Cancel his bond of life, dear God, I pray, so that I may live to say "The dog is dead."
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh, you prophesied that the time would come when I would wish for you to help me curse that bottled spider, that foul hunchbacked toad!

QUEEN MARGARET. I called you then the empty flourish of my fortune. I called you then a poor shadow, a painted queen, the mere show of what I was, the flattering preface to a dreadful pageant. One lifted high to be hurled down below, a mother only mocked with two fair babes, a dream of what you were, a gaudy flag to be the target of every dangerous shot, a sign of dignity, a breath, a bubble, a queen in jest, only to fill the scene. Where is your husband now? Where are your brothers? Where are your two sons? What do you rejoice in? Who begs, and kneels, and says "God save the Queen"? Where are the bowing peers who flattered you? Where are the thronging troops who followed you? Run through all this, and see what you are now. Instead of a happy wife, a most distressed widow. Instead of a joyful mother, one who wails the name. Instead of one who is begged from, one who humbly begs. Instead of a Queen, a wretch crowned with care. She who scorned me is now scorned by me. She who was feared by all now fears one. She who commanded all is now obeyed by none. So the course of justice has wheeled around and left you nothing but a prey to time, with only the thought of what you were to torture you more, now that you are what you are. You usurped my place, and do you not also usurp my fair share of sorrow? Now your proud neck bears half of my burdensome yoke. Right here I slip my weary head out of it and leave the whole burden on you. Farewell, York's wife, and Queen of sad misfortune. These English woes will make me smile in France.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh, you who are so skilled in curses, stay a while and teach me how to curse my enemies.

QUEEN MARGARET. Go without sleep at night, and fast by day. Compare dead happiness with living woe. Imagine that your babes were sweeter than they were, and the man who killed them fouler than he is. Making your loss better makes the one who caused it worse. Turning this over in your mind will teach you how to curse.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. My words are dull. Oh, sharpen them with yours!
QUEEN MARGARET. Your woes will make them sharp and make them pierce like mine.
[_Exit._]
DUCHESS. Why should calamity be so full of words?

QUEEN ELIZABETH. They are windy lawyers for their clients' woes, airy heirs to joys that left no will, poor breathing speakers of miseries. Let them have room. Even if what they say helps nothing else, they ease the heart.
DUCHESS. If so, then don't hold your tongue. Come with me, and in the breath of bitter words let's smother my damned son, who smothered your two sweet sons.
[_A trumpet sounds._]
The trumpet sounds. Be plentiful in your cries.
Enter King Richard and his Train, including Catesby, marching.
KING RICHARD. Who is stopping me on my march?
DUCHESS. Oh, she who could have stopped you, by strangling you in her accursed womb, from all the slaughters you have done, wretch.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Do you hide with a golden crown that forehead where, if right were right, there should be branded the slaughter of the Prince who owned that crown, and the dreadful death of my poor sons and brothers? Tell me, you villain-slave, where are my children?
DUCHESS. You toad, you toad, where is your brother Clarence, and little Ned Plantagenet, his son?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Where are the gentle Rivers, Vaughan, Grey?
DUCHESS. Where is kind Hastings?
KING RICHARD. A flourish, trumpets! Beat the alarm, drums! Don't let heaven hear these tattling women rail against the Lord's anointed. Strike, I say!
[_Flourish. Alarums._]
Either be patient and ask me politely, or I will drown your cries like this with the clamorous noise of war.
DUCHESS. Are you my son?
KING RICHARD. Yes, I thank God, my father, and yourself.
DUCHESS. Then patiently hear my impatience.
KING RICHARD. Madam, I have a touch of your temper, which can't stand the sound of reproof.
DUCHESS. Oh, let me speak!
KING RICHARD. Do, then, but I won't listen.
DUCHESS. I will be mild and gentle in my words.
KING RICHARD. And brief, good mother, for I am in a hurry.
DUCHESS. Are you in such a hurry? God knows I waited for you in torment and in agony.
KING RICHARD. And did I not come at last to comfort you?

DUCHESS. No, by the Holy Cross, you know very well you came into the world to make the world my hell. Your birth was a grievous burden to me. Your infancy was fretful and willful. Your school days were frightful, desperate, wild and furious. Your prime of manhood was daring, bold and reckless. Your mature age is proud, subtle, sly and bloody, milder but more harmful, kind in hatred. What comfortable hour can you name that ever graced me with your company?

KING RICHARD. Faith, none but Humphrey Hower, the hour that called your Grace to breakfast once, away from my company. If I am so disgraceful in your eyes, let me march on and not offend you, madam. Strike up the drum.
DUCHESS. I beg you, hear me speak.
KING RICHARD. You speak too bitterly.
DUCHESS. Hear one word, for I will never speak to you again.
KING RICHARD. So.

DUCHESS. Either you will die by God's just decree before you return from this war a conqueror, or I will perish with grief and extreme old age and never see your face again. So take with you my most grievous curse, which on the day of battle will tire you more than all the armor you wear. My prayers fight on the opposing side. There the little souls of Edward's children whisper to the spirits of your enemies and promise them success and victory. You are bloody, and bloody will be your end. Shame serves your life and attends your death.
[_Exit._]
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Though I have far more cause, I have much less spirit to curse. I say amen to her.
KING RICHARD. Wait, madam, I must have a word with you.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I have no more sons of the royal blood for you to slaughter. As for my daughters, Richard, they will be praying nuns, not weeping queens, and so don't aim to hit their lives.
KING RICHARD. You have a daughter called Elizabeth, virtuous and fair, royal and gracious.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. And must she die for this? Oh, let her live, and I'll corrupt her manners, stain her beauty, slander myself as false to Edward's bed, and throw the veil of infamy over her. So long as she may live unscarred by bloody slaughter, I will confess she was not Edward's daughter.
KING RICHARD. Don't wrong her birth. She is a royal princess.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. To save her life I'll say she is not.
KING RICHARD. Her life is safest only in her birth.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. And only in that safety did her brothers die.
KING RICHARD. Look, at their births the stars were against them.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. No, at their lives, wicked friends were against them.
KING RICHARD. The doom of destiny can't be avoided.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. True, if grace turned aside is what makes destiny. My children were destined for a better death, if grace had given you a better life.
KING RICHARD. You talk as if I had killed my cousins.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Cousins, yes, and their uncle cheated them of comfort, kingdom, family, freedom and life. Whoever's hand cut open their tender hearts, it was your head that gave the orders, though from behind. No doubt the murderer's knife was dull and blunt until it was sharpened on your stone-hard heart, so it could revel in the guts of my lambs. If constant practice in grief did not tame wild grief, my tongue would never name my boys to your ears. My nails would be dug into your eyes first, and I, in such a desperate corner of death, like a poor ship stripped of sails and rigging, would hurl myself to pieces on your rocky chest.
KING RICHARD. Madam, as I hope to thrive in my undertaking and in the dangerous outcome of these bloody wars, I mean to do more good for you and yours than you or yours were ever harmed by me!
QUEEN ELIZABETH. What good is hidden under the face of heaven, waiting to be found, that can do me any good?
KING RICHARD. The advancement of your children, gentle lady.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Up onto some scaffold, to lose their heads there.
KING RICHARD. To the dignity and height of fortune, the high imperial crown of this earth's glory.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Flatter my sorrows by telling me about it. Tell me what rank, what dignity, what honour you can hand down to any child of mine.

KING RICHARD. Everything I have, and myself too. I will give all of it to a child of yours. Then in the Lethe of your angry soul you can drown the sad memory of those wrongs you suppose I have done you.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Be brief, in case telling the story of your kindness takes longer than your kindness lasts.
KING RICHARD. Then know that I love your daughter from my soul.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Your daughter's mother thinks so too, with her soul.
KING RICHARD. What do you think?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. That you love my daughter from your soul. So from your soul's love you loved her brothers, and from my heart's love I thank you for it.
KING RICHARD. Don't be so quick to twist my meaning. I mean that I love your daughter with my soul, and I intend to make her Queen of England.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Well then, who do you mean to be her king?
KING RICHARD. The man who makes her Queen. Who else should it be?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. What, you?
KING RICHARD. Yes. What do you think of it?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. How can you court her?
KING RICHARD. That I would learn from you, since you know her moods best.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. And will you learn from me?
KING RICHARD. Madam, with all my heart.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. Send her, by the man who killed her brothers, a pair of bleeding hearts, and engrave "Edward" and "York" on them. Then perhaps she will weep. So give her as well, as Margaret once gave your father, a handkerchief soaked in Rutland's blood. Say it drained the purple sap from her sweet brothers' bodies, and tell her to wipe her weeping eyes with it. If that does not move her to love you, send her a letter about your noble deeds. Tell her you did away with her uncle Clarence and her uncle Rivers, and for her sake were quick to dispatch her good aunt Anne too.
KING RICHARD. You mock me, madam. This is no way to win your daughter.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. There is no other way, unless you could put on some other shape and not be Richard, who has done all this.
KING RICHARD. Suppose I did all this out of love for her?
QUEEN ELIZABETH. No, then she can't help hating you, since you bought love with such a bloody haul of plunder.

KING RICHARD. Look, what is done cannot be undone now. Men act rashly sometimes, and later there is time to regret it. If I took the kingdom from your sons, I'll give it to your daughter to make up for it. If I have killed the children of your womb, I will have children of my own by your daughter, so your family line grows again. A grandmother's name is hardly less loved than a mother's doting title. Grandchildren are children one step removed, of your own spirit and your own blood. The pain is the same, except for one night of groans endured by the girl whose pains you paid for in the same sorrow. Your children were a torment to your youth, but mine will be a comfort to your old age. The only thing you lose is a son being King, and by that loss your daughter is made Queen. I can't make it up to you as I would like, so accept such kindness as I can give. Your son Dorset, who walks discontented through foreign soil with a fearful soul, will be called home by this fine alliance, quickly, to high promotion and great dignity. The King who calls your beautiful daughter wife will call your Dorset brother, easily and familiarly. You will be mother to a king again, and all the ruins of these distressing times will be repaired with a double wealth of contentment. Why, we have many good days to see. The liquid drops of tears you have shed will come back transformed into eastern pearls, paying back their loan with interest, ten times double in happiness. So go, my mother, go to your daughter. Make her bashful youth bold with your experience. Prepare her ears to hear a wooer's tale. Put in her tender heart the aspiring flame of golden sovereignty. Teach the Princess about the sweet silent hours of married joy. And when this arm of mine has punished the petty rebel, dull-brained Buckingham, I will come bound with triumphant garlands and lead your daughter to a conqueror's bed. To her I will recount my conquest, and she shall be the sole victor, Caesar's Caesar.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. What would be best for me to say? That her father's brother would be her husband? Or shall I say her uncle? Or the man who killed her brothers and her uncles? Under what title shall I plead for you, so that God, the law, my honour and her love can make it seem pleasing to her tender years?
KING RICHARD. Argue that this alliance brings peace to England.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Which she will pay for with lasting war.
KING RICHARD. Tell her the King, who could command, begs.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. For something from her that the King of Kings forbids.
KING RICHARD. Say she will be a high and mighty queen.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. To lower the title in grief, as her mother does.
KING RICHARD. Say I will love her forever.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But how long will that word "forever" last?
KING RICHARD. Sweetly in force until the end of her fair life.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But how long will her sweet life fairly last?
KING RICHARD. As long as heaven and nature make it last.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. As long as hell and Richard like.
KING RICHARD. Say that I, her sovereign, am her humble servant.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. But she, your subject, hates such sovereignty.
KING RICHARD. Speak eloquently for me to her.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. An honest tale does best when told plainly.
KING RICHARD. Then tell her my loving tale plainly.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Plain but not honest is too harsh a style.
KING RICHARD. Your reasons are too shallow and too hasty.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Oh no, my reasons are too deep and dead. Too deep and dead, poor infants, in their graves.
KING RICHARD. Don't keep harping on that string, madam. That is past.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I will keep harping on it until my heartstrings break.
KING RICHARD. Now, by my George, my Garter and my crown—
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Profaned, dishonoured, and the third usurped.
KING RICHARD. I swear—

QUEEN ELIZABETH. By nothing, for this is no oath. Your George, profaned, has lost its lordly honour. Your Garter, stained, has pawned its knightly virtue. Your crown, usurped, has disgraced its kingly glory. If you want to swear something so as to be believed, swear by something you have not wronged.
KING RICHARD. Now, by the world—
QUEEN ELIZABETH. It is full of your foul wrongs.
KING RICHARD. My father's death—
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Your life has dishonoured it.
KING RICHARD. Then, by myself—
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Yourself is misused by yourself.
KING RICHARD. Why, then, by God—

QUEEN ELIZABETH. God is wronged most of all. If you had feared to break an oath with Him, you would not have broken the peace my husband the King made, and my brothers would not have died. If you had feared to break an oath by Him, the imperial gold circling your head now would have adorned my child's tender temples, and both Princes would be alive here. Instead, two tender bedfellows for dust, they are prey for worms, made so by your broken faith. What can you swear by now?
KING RICHARD. The time to come.

QUEEN ELIZABETH. You have wronged that in the time gone by. I myself will have many tears to wash the time to come, for the time past that you wronged. The children live whose fathers you slaughtered, ungoverned youths, to grieve for it in their later years. The parents live whose children you butchered, old barren plants, to grieve for it in their old age. Do not swear by the time to come, for you have misused it before using it, through the ill-used times gone by.

KING RICHARD. As I intend to prosper and repent, so may I thrive in my dangerous affairs of hostile arms! May I destroy myself! May heaven and fortune bar me from happy hours! Day, give me no light, and night, no rest! May all the planets of good luck oppose my undertakings, if I do not cherish your beautiful princely daughter with dear heart's love, spotless devotion and holy thoughts. In her lies my happiness and yours. Without her, death, desolation, ruin and decay follow for me and you, for her, for the land, and for many a Christian soul. It cannot be avoided except by this. It will not be avoided except by this. Therefore, dear mother — I must call you that — be the advocate of my love to her. Plead what I will be, not what I have been. Not my deserts, but what I will deserve. Urge the necessity and the state of the times, and don't be found petty when great plans are at stake.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Am I to be tempted by the devil like this?
KING RICHARD. Yes, if the devil tempts you to do good.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Am I to forget myself in order to be myself?
KING RICHARD. Yes, if remembering your self wrongs yourself.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Yet you killed my children.
KING RICHARD. But in your daughter's womb I bury them. In that nest of spices they will breed new selves of themselves, to comfort you again.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. Am I to go and win my daughter to your will?
KING RICHARD. And be a happy mother by the deed.
QUEEN ELIZABETH. I go. Write to me very soon, and you will learn her mind from me.
KING RICHARD. Take her a kiss from my true love, and so, farewell.
[_Kissing her. Exit Queen Elizabeth._]
Relenting fool, and shallow, changing woman!
Enter Ratcliffe.
How now, what news?

RATCLIFFE. Most mighty sovereign, a powerful fleet is riding off the west coast. Many doubtful, hollow-hearted friends are crowding to our shores, unarmed and undecided about driving them back. People think Richmond is their admiral. They are drifting out there, waiting only for Buckingham's help to welcome them ashore.
KING RICHARD. Some fast-footed friend, ride to the Duke of Norfolk. Ratcliffe, you go yourself, or Catesby. Where is he?
CATESBY. Here, my good lord.
KING RICHARD. Catesby, fly to the Duke.
CATESBY. I will, my lord, with all convenient haste.
KING RICHARD. Ratcliffe, come here. Ride to Salisbury. When you get there—
[_To Catesby._] Dull, forgetful villain,
why are you standing here and not going to the Duke?
CATESBY. First, mighty lord, tell me what Your Highness wants, what I am to deliver to him from Your Grace.
KING RICHARD. Oh, true, good Catesby. Tell him to raise at once the greatest force he can muster, and meet me quickly at Salisbury.
CATESBY. I go.
[_Exit._]
RATCLIFFE. What, if it please you, shall I do at Salisbury?
KING RICHARD. Why, what would you do there before I go?
RATCLIFFE. Your Highness told me to ride ahead.
KING RICHARD. I've changed my mind.
Enter Stanley Earl of Derby.
Stanley, what news do you bring?
STANLEY. None good, my lord, that would please you to hear. And none so bad that it can't be reported.
KING RICHARD. Well, a riddle! Neither good nor bad. Why do you run so many miles around when you can tell your tale the shortest way? Once more, what news?
STANLEY. Richmond is on the seas.
KING RICHARD. Let him sink there, and let the seas close over him! The white-livered runaway, what is he doing there?
STANLEY. I don't know, mighty sovereign, except by guessing.
KING RICHARD. Well, as you guess?
STANLEY. Stirred up by Dorset, Buckingham and Morton, he is heading for England to claim the crown.

KING RICHARD. Is the throne empty? Is the sword left unswung? Is the King dead? Is the kingdom unclaimed? What heir of York is alive except me? And who is England's King but great York's heir? Then tell me, what is he doing on the seas?
STANLEY. Unless it's for that, my lord, I can't guess.
KING RICHARD. Unless he comes to be your lord, you can't guess why the Welshman is coming. I fear you will rebel and fly to him.
STANLEY. No, my good lord. So don't mistrust me.
KING RICHARD. Where is your army, then, to beat him back? Where are your tenants and your followers? Aren't they on the western shore right now, escorting the rebels safely from their ships?
STANLEY. No, my good lord, my friends are in the north.
KING RICHARD. Cold friends to me. What are they doing in the north, when they should be serving their sovereign in the west?
STANLEY. They have not been ordered, mighty King. If it please Your Majesty to give me leave, I'll gather my friends and meet Your Grace wherever and whenever Your Majesty wishes.
KING RICHARD. Yes, yes, you'd like to be gone to join Richmond. But I won't trust you.
STANLEY. Most mighty sovereign, you have no reason to doubt my friendship. I never was false and never will be.
KING RICHARD. Go then, and gather men, but leave behind your son George Stanley. Make sure your heart is firm, or else the safety of his head is frail.
STANLEY. Treat him according to how I prove true to you.
[_Exit._]
Enter a Messenger.

MESSENGER. My gracious sovereign, I am well informed by friends that in Devonshire Sir Edward Courtney and his elder brother, the haughty prelate Bishop of Exeter, are in arms with many more confederates.
Enter another Messenger.
SECOND MESSENGER. In Kent, my lord, the Guilfords are in arms. Every hour more allies flock to the rebels, and their strength grows.
Enter another Messenger.
THIRD MESSENGER. My lord, the army of great Buckingham—
KING RICHARD. Out on you, owls! Is it nothing but songs of death?
[_He strikes him._]
There, take that until you bring better news.

THIRD MESSENGER. The news I have to tell Your Majesty is that sudden floods and rising waters have scattered and dispersed Buckingham's army. He himself has wandered off alone, and no one knows where.
KING RICHARD. I beg your pardon. Here is my purse to cure that blow. Has some well-advised friend proclaimed a reward for whoever brings the traitor in?
THIRD MESSENGER. Such a proclamation has been made, my lord.
Enter another Messenger.

FOURTH MESSENGER. Sir Thomas Lovell and Lord Marquess Dorset, it's said, my lord, are in arms in Yorkshire. But I bring Your Highness this good comfort: a tempest has scattered the Breton fleet. Richmond, off Dorsetshire, sent a boat to the shore to ask those on the banks whether they were his supporters, yes or no. They answered that they came from Buckingham, on his side. Mistrusting them, he hoisted sail and set his course again for Brittany.
KING RICHARD. March on, march on, since we are up in arms. If not to fight foreign enemies, then at least to beat down these rebels here at home.
Enter Catesby.
CATESBY. My lord, the Duke of Buckingham is captured. That is the best news. That the Earl of Richmond has landed at Milford with a mighty force is colder tidings, yet they must be told.
KING RICHARD. Away towards Salisbury! While we talk here, a royal battle might be won and lost. Someone see that Buckingham is brought to Salisbury. The rest march on with me.
[_Flourish. Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — A Room in Lord Stanley’s house
paragraphs: Enter Stanley Earl of Derby and Sir Christopher Urswick.

STANLEY. Sir Christopher, tell Richmond this from me. My son George Stanley is penned up in the sty of the most deadly boar. If I revolt, young George's head comes off. Fear of that holds back my help for now. So be on your way. Give my regards to your lord. Tell him as well that the Queen has heartily agreed that he should marry her daughter Elizabeth. But tell me, where is princely Richmond now?
CHRISTOPHER. At Pembroke, or at Haverfordwest in Wales.
STANLEY. What men of note are joining him?

CHRISTOPHER. Sir Walter Herbert, a renowned soldier; Sir Gilbert Talbot, Sir William Stanley, Oxford, the redoubtable Pembroke, Sir James Blunt, and Rice ap Thomas with a valiant crew, and many others of great name and worth. They are heading their forces toward London, unless they are fought on the way.
STANLEY. Well, hurry to your lord. I kiss his hand. My letter will tell him my mind. Farewell.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Salisbury. An open place
paragraphs: Enter Sheriff and Halberds, with Buckingham, led to execution.
BUCKINGHAM. Won't King Richard let me speak with him?
SHERIFF. No, my good lord, so be patient.

BUCKINGHAM. Hastings, and Edward's children, Grey and Rivers, holy King Henry and your fair son Edward, Vaughan, and all of you who died through underhanded, corrupt, foul injustice: if your moody, discontented souls look down through the clouds on this present hour, then mock my destruction, as your revenge. This is All Souls' Day, fellow, isn't it?
SHERIFF. It is.

BUCKINGHAM. Why, then All Souls' Day is my body's doomsday. In King Edward's time, this is the day I wished would fall on me if I were found false to his children and his wife's allies. This is the day I wished would fall on me through the false faith of the man I trusted most. This, this All Souls' Day, for my fearful soul, is the appointed end to my wrongs. That high All-Seer I trifled with has turned my pretended prayer back on my head and granted in earnest what I begged in jest. So He forces the swords of wicked men to turn their points against their masters' breasts. So Margaret's curse falls heavy on my neck: "When he," she said, "splits your heart with sorrow, remember Margaret was a prophetess." Come, officers, lead me to the block of shame. Wrong gets only wrong, and blame gets the blame it is due.
[_Exit with Officers._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — Plain near Tamworth
paragraphs: Enter Richmond, Oxford, Blunt, Herbert, and others, with drum and colours.

RICHMOND. Fellow soldiers and my most loving friends, bruised under the yoke of tyranny: we have marched this far into the heart of the land without any obstacle. And here we get from our stepfather Stanley lines of fair comfort and encouragement. The wretched, bloody, usurping boar has ruined your summer fields and fruitful vines. He swills your warm blood like slops and makes his trough in your ripped-open chests. This foul swine is now right in the middle of this island, near the town of Leicester, as we learn. From Tamworth it is only one day's march there. In God's name, press on cheerfully, courageous friends, to reap the harvest of lasting peace through this one bloody trial of sharp war.
OXFORD. Every man's conscience is worth a thousand men in a fight against that guilty murderer.
HERBERT. I don't doubt his friends will turn to us.
BLUNT. He has no friends except friends out of fear, and in his greatest need they will fly from him.
RICHMOND. All to our advantage. Then in God's name, march. True hope is swift and flies on swallow's wings. It makes kings into gods, and lesser creatures into kings.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Bosworth Field
paragraphs: Enter King Richard in arms, with Norfolk, Ratcliffe  and the Earl of Surrey with others.
KING RICHARD. Pitch our tent here, right here in Bosworth field. My Lord of Surrey, why do you look so sad?
SURREY. My heart is ten times lighter than my looks.
KING RICHARD. My lord of Norfolk.
NORFOLK. Here, most gracious lord.
KING RICHARD. Norfolk, we must have blows, ha, must we not?
NORFOLK. We must both give and take, my loving lord.
KING RICHARD. Put up my tent! I'll lie here tonight. But where tomorrow? Well, that makes no difference. Who has counted the number of the traitors?
NORFOLK. Six or seven thousand is their full strength.

KING RICHARD. Why, our army is triple that. Besides, the King's name is a tower of strength, which the enemy side lacks. Put up the tent! Come, noble gentlemen, let's survey the lie of the land for our advantage. Call for some men of sound judgment. Let's lack no discipline and make no delay, for, lords, tomorrow is a busy day.
[_The tent is now ready. Exeunt._]
Enter Richmond, Sir William Brandon, Oxford, Herbert, Blunt, and others who pitch Richmond’s tent.

RICHMOND. The weary sun has made a golden setting, and by the bright track of his fiery chariot he promises a fine day tomorrow. Sir William Brandon, you shall carry my standard. Give me some ink and paper in my tent. I'll draw up the plan and layout of our battle, assign each leader his own command, and divide our small force in fair proportions. My Lord of Oxford, you, Sir William Brandon, and you, Sir Walter Herbert, stay with me. The Earl of Pembroke is staying with his regiment. Good Captain Blunt, take my goodnight to him, and ask the Earl to see me in my tent by the second hour of the morning. Yet one more thing, good captain, do for me. Where is Lord Stanley quartered, do you know?
BLUNT. Unless I have badly mistaken his colours, which I am sure I have not, his regiment lies at least half a mile south of the King's mighty army.
RICHMOND. If it can be done without danger, sweet Blunt, find some good way to speak with him, and give him this most needed note from me.
BLUNT. On my life, my lord, I'll undertake it. And so may God give you quiet rest tonight.
RICHMOND. Good night, good Captain Blunt.
[_Exit Blunt._]
Come, gentlemen, let us consult about tomorrow's business. Into my tent. The dew is raw and cold.
[_Richmond, Brandon Herbert, and  Oxford withdraw into the tent. The others exeunt._]
Enter to his tent, King Richard, Ratcliffe, Norfolk and Catesby with Soldiers.
KING RICHARD. What time is it?
CATESBY. It's suppertime, my lord. It's nine o'clock.
KING RICHARD. I won't eat supper tonight. Give me some ink and paper. What, is my helmet visor easier than it was? And is all my armour laid in my tent?
CATESBY. It is, my lord, and everything is ready.
KING RICHARD. Good Norfolk, hurry to your post. Keep careful watch. Choose trustworthy sentries.
NORFOLK. I go, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Be up with the lark tomorrow, gentle Norfolk.
NORFOLK. I promise you, my lord.
[_Exit._]
KING RICHARD. Catesby!
CATESBY. My lord?
KING RICHARD. Send an officer-at-arms to Stanley's regiment. Tell him to bring his force before sunrise, or his son George will fall into the blind cave of eternal night.
[_Exit Catesby._]
Fill me a bowl of wine. Give me a watch. Saddle white Surrey for the field tomorrow. Make sure my lances are sound and not too heavy. Ratcliffe!
RATCLIFFE. My lord?
KING RICHARD. Did you see the melancholy Lord Northumberland?
RATCLIFFE. Thomas, the Earl of Surrey, and he went through the army from troop to troop around dusk, cheering up the soldiers.
KING RICHARD. Good, I'm satisfied. Give me a bowl of wine. I don't have the liveliness of spirit or cheer of mind that I used to have. Set it down. Are ink and paper ready?
RATCLIFFE. They are, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Tell my guard to keep watch, and leave me. Ratcliffe, come to my tent around midnight and help me arm. Leave me, I say.
[_Exit Ratcliffe. Richard withdraws into his tent; attendant soldiers guard it_.]
Enter Stanley Earl of Derby to Richmond in his tent.
STANLEY. May fortune and victory sit on your helmet!
RICHMOND. May all the comfort the dark night can give be yours, noble stepfather. Tell me, how is our loving mother?

STANLEY. I bless you on behalf of your mother, as her stand-in. She prays constantly for Richmond's good. So much for that. The silent hours steal on, and flaky darkness breaks in the east. In short, since the moment demands it, prepare your army early in the morning and put your fortune to the judgment of bloody blows and deadly-staring war.
