I will, as I can, deceive the moment to the best advantage and help you in this uncertain clash of arms. What I would like to do, I cannot. But I may not be too forward on your side, or your brother, tender George, would be executed in his father's sight. Farewell. The lack of time and the fearful moment cut short the ceremonious vows of love and the long exchange of sweet talk that friends so long parted should linger over. God give us leisure for these rites of love! Once more, goodbye. Be valiant, and may you succeed.

RICHMOND. Good lords, escort him to his regiment. I'll struggle with my troubled thoughts to take a nap, so that leaden sleep doesn't weigh me down tomorrow, when I should rise on the wings of victory. Once more, good night, kind lords and gentlemen.
[_All but Richmond leave his tent._]
[_Kneels_.] Oh You, whose captain I count myself,

look on my forces with a gracious eye. Put in their hands Your bruising irons of wrath, so that they crush with a heavy fall the usurping helmets of our enemies. Make us Your ministers of punishment, so that we may praise You in the victory. To You I commend my watchful soul before I let the windows of my eyes fall shut. Sleeping and waking, oh, defend me still!
[_Sleeps._]
Enter the Ghost of young Prince Edward, son to Harry the Sixth.
GHOST OF EDWARD.
[_To King Richard._] Let me weigh heavy on your soul tomorrow.
Think how you stabbed me in my prime of youth at Tewksbury. Therefore despair and die!
[_To Richmond._] Be cheerful, Richmond, for the wronged souls
of butchered princes fight on your behalf. King Henry's descendant, Richmond, comforts you.
[_Exit._]
Enter the Ghost of Henry the Sixth.
GHOST OF HENRY.
[_To King Richard._] When I was mortal, my anointed body
was punched full of deadly holes by you. Think on the Tower and me. Despair and die! Harry the Sixth tells you to despair and die.
[_To Richmond._] Virtuous and holy, be the conqueror.
Harry, who prophesied that you would be King, comforts you in your sleep. Live and flourish!
[_Exit._]
Enter the Ghost of Clarence.
GHOST OF CLARENCE.
[_To King Richard._] Let me weigh heavy on your soul tomorrow,
I who was washed to death with foul wine, poor Clarence, betrayed to death by your guile. Tomorrow in the battle think on me, and let your edgeless sword fall. Despair and die!
[_To Richmond._] You offspring of the house of Lancaster,
the wronged heirs of York pray for you. May good angels guard your battle. Live and flourish.
[_Exit._]
Enter the Ghosts of Rivers, Grey and Vaughan.
GHOST OF RIVERS.
[_To King Richard._] Let me weigh heavy on your soul tomorrow,
Rivers, who died at Pomfret. Despair and die!
GHOST OF GREY.
[_To King Richard._] Think upon Grey, and let your soul despair!
GHOST OF VAUGHAN.
[_To King Richard._] Think upon Vaughan, and with guilty fear
let your lance fall. Despair and die!
ALL THREE.
[_To Richmond._] Awake, and think how our wrongs in Richard's chest
will conquer him. Awake, and win the day.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter the Ghost of Hastings.
GHOST OF HASTINGS.
[_To King Richard._] Bloody and guilty, wake up guilty,
and end your days in a bloody battle. Think on Lord Hastings. Despair and die!
[_To Richmond._] Quiet, untroubled soul, awake, awake.
Arm, fight and conquer for fair England's sake.
[_Exit._]
Enter the Ghosts of the two young Princes.
GHOSTS OF PRINCES.
[_To King Richard._] Dream on about your nephews, smothered in the Tower.
Let us be lead inside your chest, Richard, and weigh you down to ruin, shame and death. Your nephews' souls tell you to despair and die.
[_To Richmond._] Sleep, Richmond, sleep in peace, and wake in joy.
May good angels guard you from the boar's harm. Live, and father a happy line of kings. Edward's unhappy sons tell you to flourish.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter the Ghost of Lady Anne, his wife.
GHOST OF ANNE.
[_To King Richard._] Richard, your wife, that wretched Anne your wife,
who never slept a quiet hour with you, now fills your sleep with disturbances. Tomorrow in the battle think on me, and let your edgeless sword fall. Despair and die!
[_To Richmond._] You quiet soul, sleep a quiet sleep.
Dream of success and happy victory. Your enemy's wife prays for you.
[_Exit._]
Enter the Ghost of Buckingham.
GHOST OF BUCKINGHAM.
[_To King Richard._] I was the first to help you to the crown,

and the last to feel your tyranny. Oh, in the battle think on Buckingham, and die in terror of your guilt. Dream on, dream on of bloody deeds and death. Fainting, despair. Despairing, give up your breath.
[_To Richmond._] I died in hope before I could lend you aid,
but cheer your heart, and don't be dismayed. God and good angels fight on Richmond's side, and may Richard fall at the height of all his pride.
[_Exit._]
[_King Richard starts up out of his dream._]

KING RICHARD. Give me another horse! Bind up my wounds! Have mercy, Jesus! — Wait! I only dreamed. Oh coward conscience, how you torment me! The lights burn blue. It is now dead midnight. Cold, fearful drops stand on my trembling flesh. What do I fear? Myself? There's no one else here. Richard loves Richard, that is, I am I. Is there a murderer here? No. Yes, I am. Then fly. What, from myself? There's a good reason: in case I take revenge. What, myself on myself? Alas, I love myself. Why? For any good I myself have done to myself? Oh no, alas, I rather hate myself for hateful deeds done by myself. I am a villain. Yet I lie, I am not. Fool, speak well of yourself. Fool, don't flatter. My conscience has a thousand different tongues, and every tongue brings in a different tale, and every tale condemns me as a villain. Perjury, perjury, in the highest degree. Murder, stern murder, in the direst degree. All the different sins, all committed in every degree, throng to the bar, all crying "Guilty, guilty!" I shall despair. There is no creature who loves me, and if I die no soul will pity me. And why should they, since I myself find no pity in myself for myself? I thought the souls of all those I had murdered came to my tent, and every one threatened tomorrow's vengeance on Richard's head.
Enter Ratcliffe.
RATCLIFFE. My lord!
KING RICHARD. Damn it! Who's there?
RATCLIFFE. Ratcliffe, my lord. It's me. The early village cock has crowed twice to greet the morning. Your friends are up and buckling on their armour.
KING RICHARD. Oh Ratcliffe, I have dreamed a fearful dream! What do you think, will all our friends prove true?
RATCLIFFE. No doubt, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Oh Ratcliffe, I fear, I fear!
RATCLIFFE. No, my good lord, don't be afraid of shadows.

KING RICHARD. By the apostle Paul, shadows tonight have struck more terror into Richard's soul than ten thousand soldiers in proven armour, led by shallow Richmond, could. It's not yet near day. Come, go with me. I'll play the eavesdropper among our tents, to see if anyone means to shrink from me.
[_Exeunt Richard and Ratcliffe._]
Enter the Lords to Richmond in his tent.
LORDS. Good morning, Richmond.
RICHMOND. Forgive me, lords and watchful gentlemen, for letting you find a late sluggard here.
LORDS. How did you sleep, my lord?

RICHMOND. Since you left, my lords, I have had the sweetest sleep and the most promising dreams that ever entered a drowsy head. I thought the souls of those whose bodies Richard murdered came to my tent and cheered for victory. I promise you, my heart is very cheerful at the memory of so fair a dream. How far into the morning is it, lords?
LORDS. Just striking four.
RICHMOND. Why, then it's time to arm and give orders.
His oration to his soldiers.

Loving countrymen, the lack of time and the pressure of the moment forbid me to say more than I have. Yet remember this. God and our good cause fight on our side. The prayers of holy saints and wronged souls stand before us like high-built walls. Except for Richard, those we fight against would rather have us win than the man they follow. For what is he they follow? Truly, gentlemen, a bloody tyrant and a murderer. One raised in blood and established in blood. One who schemed to get what he has and slaughtered those who helped him get it. A base, foul stone, made precious only by the foil of England's throne, where he is falsely set. One who has always been God's enemy. Then, if you fight God's enemy, God will in justice protect you as his soldiers. If you sweat to put a tyrant down, you will sleep in peace once the tyrant is slain. If you fight your country's foes, your country's riches will pay you for your pains. If you fight to protect your wives, your wives will welcome home the conquerors. If you free your children from the sword, your children's children will repay you in your old age. Then, in the name of God and all these rights, advance your standards and draw your willing swords. As for me, the price of my bold attempt will be this cold corpse on the earth's cold face. But if I thrive, even the least of you will share in the gain of my attempt. Sound drums and trumpets boldly and cheerfully! God and Saint George! Richmond and victory!
[_Exeunt._]
Enter King Richard, Ratcliffe and Soldiers.
KING RICHARD. What did Northumberland say about Richmond?
RATCLIFFE. That he was never trained in arms.
KING RICHARD. He told the truth. And what did Surrey say then?
RATCLIFFE. He smiled, and said, "All the better for our purpose."
KING RICHARD. He was right, and so it is.
[_The clock striketh._]
Count the clock there. Give me an almanac. Who saw the sun today?
RATCLIFFE. Not I, my lord.
KING RICHARD. Then he refuses to shine, for according to the book he should have braved the east an hour ago. It will be a black day for somebody. Ratcliffe!
RATCLIFFE. My lord?

KING RICHARD. The sun will not be seen today! The sky frowns and glowers upon our army. I wish these dewy tears were off the ground. Not shine today? Why, what is that to me any more than to Richmond? The very same heaven that frowns on me looks sadly on him.
Enter Norfolk.
NORFOLK. Arm, arm, my lord. The enemy is boasting in the field.

KING RICHARD. Come, bustle, bustle! Put the armour on my horse. Call up Lord Stanley and tell him to bring his force. I will lead my soldiers out onto the plain, and this is how my battle will be arranged. My vanguard will be drawn out in a long line, made up equally of cavalry and infantry. Our archers will be placed in the middle. John Duke of Norfolk and Thomas Earl of Surrey will command this infantry and cavalry. With them so directed, we will follow in the main battle, whose strength will be well flanked on either side by our best cavalry. This, and Saint George besides! What do you think, Norfolk?
NORFOLK. A good plan, warlike sovereign.
[_He sheweth him a paper._]
I found this on my tent this morning.
KING RICHARD.
[_Reads_.] "Jockey of Norfolk, be not too bold.

For Dickon your master is bought and sold." A thing devised by the enemy. Go, gentlemen, every man to his command. Don't let our babbling dreams frighten our souls. Conscience is only a word that cowards use, invented at first to keep the strong in awe. Let our strong arms be our conscience and swords our law. March on. Join the fight bravely. Let's go at it pell-mell, and if not to heaven, then hand in hand to hell.
His oration to his army.

What more shall I say than I have already suggested? Remember whom you have to deal with: a bunch of vagabonds, rascals and runaways, a scum of Bretons and base lackey peasants, whom their overstuffed country vomits out to desperate adventures and certain destruction. While you sleep safe, they bring you unrest. You have lands and are blessed with beautiful wives. They would seize the one and dishonour the other. And who leads them but a paltry fellow, long kept in Brittany at the expense of our mother country? A milksop, who never in his life felt more cold than snow over his shoes? Let's whip these stragglers back across the sea, lash away these overweening rags of France, these starving beggars weary of their lives. If they had not dreamed up this foolish exploit, poor rats, they would have hanged themselves for lack of means. If we are to be conquered, let men conquer us, not these bastard Bretons, whom our fathers beat, mocked and thumped in their own land, and left on the record as heirs of shame. Shall these men enjoy our lands? Sleep with our wives? Rape our daughters?
[_Drum afar off._]

Listen, I hear their drum. Fight, gentlemen of England! Fight, bold yeomen! Draw, archers, draw your arrows to the head! Spur your proud horses hard, and ride in blood! Stun the heavens with your splintering lances!
Enter a Messenger.
What does Lord Stanley say? Will he bring his army?
MESSENGER. My lord, he refuses to come.
KING RICHARD. Cut off the head of his son George!
NORFOLK. My lord, the enemy has crossed the marsh. Let George Stanley die after the battle.

KING RICHARD. I feel a thousand hearts swelling in my chest. Raise our banners! Attack our enemies! Let our old battle cry, good Saint George, fill us with the fury of fiery dragons! Charge them! Victory sits on our helmets.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Another part of the Field
paragraphs: Alarum. Excursions. Enter Norfolk and Soldiers; to him Catesby.

CATESBY. Help, my lord of Norfolk, help, help! The King is doing more than any man could. He dares to face every danger. His horse is killed, and he fights on foot, hunting for Richmond in the very throat of death. Help, good lord, or the day is lost!
[_Exeunt Norfolk and Soldiers._]
Alarum. Enter King Richard.
KING RICHARD. A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!
CATESBY. Get back, my lord. I'll help you find a horse.

KING RICHARD. Slave, I have staked my life on one throw, and I will take whatever the dice give. I think there are six Richmonds on this field. I have killed five of them today instead of him. A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Another part of the Field
paragraphs: Alarum. Enter King Richard and Richmond. They fight. Richard is slain. Then retreat being sounded. Richmond exits, and Richard's body is carried off. Flourish. Enter Richmond, Stanley Earl of Derby, bearing the crown, with other Lords and Soldiers.
RICHMOND. God and your arms be praised, victorious friends! The day is ours. The bloody dog is dead.

STANLEY. Brave Richmond, you have done well! Look, here is the crown that was held unlawfully for so long. I have pulled it off the dead head of this bloody wretch to set it on your brow. Wear it, enjoy it, and value it.
RICHMOND. Great God of heaven, say Amen to all of it! But tell me, is young George Stanley alive?
STANLEY. He is, my lord, and safe in the town of Leicester. If you like, we can go there now.
RICHMOND. Which men of rank were killed on either side?
STANLEY. John, Duke of Norfolk; Walter, Lord Ferrers; Sir Robert Brakenbury; and Sir William Brandon.

RICHMOND. Bury their bodies as their rank deserves. Announce a pardon for the soldiers who ran away, if they come back and submit to us. Then, as we have taken the sacrament to do, we will unite the white rose and the red. May heaven smile on this union, after frowning so long on their hatred. What traitor hears me and does not say Amen? England has been mad for a long time and has torn her own flesh. Brother blindly shed brother's blood. Fathers rashly killed their own sons. Sons, forced to it, became their fathers' butchers. All this split York and Lancaster apart in their terrible quarrel. Oh, now let Richmond and Elizabeth, the true heirs of each royal house, be joined together by God's good ordinance. And let their children, God, if it is Your will, fill the time to come with gentle peace, smiling plenty and prosperous days. Blunt the blade of traitors, gracious Lord, who would bring back these bloody days and make poor England weep rivers of blood. Do not let them live to enjoy this land's harvest, if they would wound this land's peace with treason. Now the wounds of civil war are closed, and peace lives again. May she live here long. God, say Amen.
[_Exeunt._]
